subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, time forbids that I make any extended references to the speeches already made during this debate. One of the most notable, I think, was the address of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). It was a notable speech in that it struck a new note and indicated a new viewpoint coming from the treasury benches, and I think we may hope that it will become the basis, in the not far distant future, of an entirely different policy in this country. Worthy also of much study and discussion was the speech made by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) yesterday afternoon, which was an able defence of the amendment moved from this corner of the house and an interpretation of the financial system, and which contained suggestions as to how we might get out of
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

our present economic difficulty. I should like also, to offer my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) who, for his many good qualities, is very highly respected in this house. I regret that the world situation, and particularly the economic situation in Canada, should have been such as to make difficult the presentation of his first budget.
I should like also to offer a word of congratulation to the government. As is well known, I hold very different views, both on questions of economics and politics, from those to which expression has been given in the policies of this government, as well as in the policies of preceding governments. Nevertheless, I am not unmindful of the colossal task confronting this administration at the present time, and in view of that fact I will not snarl at the heels of the government. Civilization to-day is in the process of a readjustment so fundamental in character as ultimately to leave untouched no field of knowledge or of experience, nor any institution without at least some modification. In Canada, as in other countries, we are confronted with a situation for which history offers no parallel. Therefore we must face this fact, that there are no precedents which we can fittingly apply, and we must work our way out by doing things which no one knows how to do because they have never been done before. In view of all this I gladly congratulate the government on its able leadership, its honest administration, its decisive and at times courageous actions and its sincere devotion to the well-being of the nation. But when all these things have been said and acknowledged it does not by any means follow that success has been secured. In other words I have no criticism of the captain of our ship, Canada, in so far as his ability as a navigator is concerned. I have no criticism of his seamanship or of the character and ability of his crew. The objection I am going to register to-day is with the direction in which the ship is going and the port towards which it is bound.
I want to direct my attention particularly, Mr. Speaker, to the subamendment moved from this corner of the house. As will be seen by hon. members, this subamendment is a challenge to the existing system, and I had hoped that the debate which followed would have been on that issue and that some difference of opinion would have been offered either with regard to the statements of fact included in the subamendment, the opinions expressed as to the proper interpretation of the economic situation, or to the proposals themselves.

With regard to the amendment I have to say that I look upon it as supporting the budget, since it takes exception only to what to my mind is an infinitesimal detail in the great national policy and attributes to that detail all the present difficulties of our economic life. Since it takes exception to only one small detail in the budget I assume that those moving it are perfectly satisfied with the system as a whole, and so far as I am concerned the amendment by implication really supports the budget. The subamendment, however, unqualifiedly declares that it does not think the present capitalistic system can be salvaged in its present form but that definite modifications are necessary, and so I should like to direct the attention of the house first to the statements of fact contained in the subamendment.
In the subamendment it is stated that there is an ample supply of natural resources to provide the people of Canada with all the primary needs of life: that we have sufficient and efficient industrial machinery, including plant equipment and skilled workers which, if applied to the natural resources, could produce all that we require in Canada. Further it is said that notwithstanding these facts our debts, personal, social and national, are increasing. These are facts that have not been challenged by anyone during the course of this debate, and I question whether anyone will have the temerity to challenge them. They are too obvious to the people at large; they cannot be challenged. Then, with these facts before us, we express the opinion that since this is the case, and our people are hungry and without work or economic hope, the trouble is to be found in the economic system itself. No one has challenged that opinion. It is only an opinion, and I admit that it may be challenged successfully, but so far no one has said there is not some defect in an economic system capable of producing the results enumerated.
Then we come to the next step; having emphasized the importance of finance in the national policy to-day we offer the suggestion, as a first step towards a solution of the economic problem facing the people of Canada, that there should be a nationalization of the credit system of this country. The hon. member for Macleod dealt specifically with that part of our subamendment yesterday, so I will not deal with it further at this time, but will rather turn my attention to the general viewpoint which the subamendment seeks to envisage with regard to the economic conditions with which it deals.

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
The budget itself, the subject of all our discussion, and in connection with which our subamendment has been moved, to my mind is a very true reflex of the psychological condition of the country in respect of our economic problem. It is a budget exactly the same in all major respects as other budgets presented by various governments of the world. These are the outstanding characteristics of the budget. It reveals a marked decline in trade, a falling-off of revenue, a reduction of public services, increased taxation, a reduction in the salaries of public servants and an increase in debt. I am not blaming the government for all these dismal things; I am merely enumerating what the budget discloses to us and to the people of Canada and pointing out the idea which it reflects that there is great necessity in this country for curtailment of expenditures, for curtailment of purchasing power-that for some reason or other we ought to be taking care of our wealth instead of using it.
Now, the budget as a whole presents one issue in particular to which I wish to call attention. That issue is this: Shall this government, shall this parliament, shall this people of Canada be controlled by money or shall it control money? That is not to say that some individuals of great wealth determine the policy of governments, but it is to say that the monetary system is accepted both by parliament and by the people as a sacred institution to be preserved at all costs; and once that is accepted then the factors which I have enumerated as appearing in the budget become, under present conditions, inevitable.
Let me call the attention of this house and of the country to the tragedy of waste which this policy, reflected in the budget, means. There seems to be a desire to save. Well, I am interested in what we are trying to save. Are we really practising a form of economy which will save the real wealth of the nation or are we being penny wise and pound foolish? While we are saving figures in a book, through the present system of book-keeping, while we are curtailing expenditures as the budget provides, what about the waste of the machine that is standing idle? What about the waste of the great surplus of goods which no one is able to use because they cannot be bought? What about the waste of human values-the unemployed who are hopelessly walking the streets? What about the waste of youth looking forward in hopefulness to find some expression for their best selves in Canada? What about them? These are the things we ought to be conserving; these are the places where we ought to practise economy. But we cannot save these things while practising
this form of economy under the present financial system.
It has been said by many that this is a dollar civilization, that the dollar has been regarded as the god of our age. If this was ever true it is more true to-day than at any other time in the world's history. Canada, like other nations, sits in sackcloth and ashes, offering her sacrifices to the dollar deity. Every luxury denied to the Canadian people in the face of the present abundance is a sacrifice to the dollar deity. Every curtailment of public services, the great mass of the unemployed, the comfort denied the masses of the people, the very necessities of life denied to many-these are all in the line of sacrifices to a book-keeping system. I am reminded of an incident in the history of the great Jewidh people. When Moses took a holiday, he found on his return that there had been great disruption in the camp, and the people were worshipping a golden calf. He sent for Aaron to explain the situation and Aaron, trying to make some excuse, said that the people had put all their treasures into the fire, and, lo, this calf had come forth. It seems to me that this is about what we are trying to do in Canada to-day: We are pouring all our treasures, out real wealth, our human values, into the fire of the present financial system, and I fear that the only thing that will come out will be a calf. I protest against such sacrifices, especially when economic abundance renders the performance absurd.
The dollar is an invention of mankind for convenience in the exchange of goods, and I hope that Canada will not for long bow the knee to it nor acknowledge it as the sacred dictator of a sacrificial policy unnecessarily imposed upon the people. This policy of rigid economy is due, perhaps, to certain deep-rooted psychological causes as well as economic. I think that we might divide the honours or the dishonours between instinctive and paralyzing fear and lack of vision on the part of this house and of the country at large. That fear is the fear of scarcity, and I presume it was generated at a time when the world ,was Teally in danger of real scarcity, when the tooth and claw method was necessary to survive; and unfortunately for us it appears that instinct does not respond as readily to a new set of circumstances as does intelligence. Instinct has a tendency to go on in a straight line while intelligence notes all the facts of a changed situation. And so it is to-day that we, in spite of the abundance which we are conscious of possessing, go on in a straight line towards scarcity, hampering and
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

hindering the distribution of goods which we have already been able to produce. The fear psychology is gradually developing. Capitalists are afraid that capitalism will collapse, and the socialists and those who are usually termed reds, all opposed to the capitalistic system, are afraid that it will not collapse, which might be a greater tragedy than the other. At any rate, all are afraid of some danger. Even Mr. Wells, in one of his writings, expresses the view that civilization is a race between catastrophe and knowledge, and then later he calls the race off because, as he says, there is not enough knowledge to make a race. I disagree with him in his implication, for he implies that civilization has been built without intelligence, and I fail to see how civilization built without intelligence will ever be destroyed by lack of it. However, from Dean Inge and H. G. Wells to the vociferous and ubiquitous communist agitator, they all encourage us to anticipate disaster, until we have developed what we might call an appetite for disaster, which seems to want to satisfy itself.
After all, what is there to fear? We are told that a crash is about to come; and when we read the words which Sir Montagu Norman addressed to some official in France, we can almost hear the reverberations of that great crash. But what is there to crash? The only thing that can crash is our way of doing things-a way which is not doing them very well, a way of doing things which may be standing in the way of better ways of doing things. The only thing that can crash, I say, is our -present system, our method of doing things. The greatest crash would come from the debts of the world, and those of us who are burdened that way do not anticipate that with any sort of disfavour. Let it crash; there is nothing to fear in that.
Capitalism itself is only an incident in the evolution of economics. Economics and all that it stands for will be here when capitalism is gone. But of course there is always danger, for life itself is the most dangerous of all experiments. There are dangers which are usually as great as the achievements with which they are associated. The magnetic compass has been responsible for the death by drowning of mariners in the "Devil's Hole" and of struggles for life in the "Roaring Forties." Every mile that Columbus sailed carried him further in the path of danger; yet he discovered a world. The first aviator faced great danger but he conquered the air. If we are to stand on the threshold of a new age, merely contemplating the dangers ahead, we shall fail in our great achievement. Some

hon. members of the house may disagree with my colleagues and myself when we say that we believe we are on the threshold of a new social order, but we will be permitted to express our views at least. Things cannot go on as they have been going. We cannot express too much our opinion in that regard; we should not shiver in fear but we should look at the great possibilities and contemplate the achievements rather than the dangers which may be entailed.
Let me direct the attention of the house to some elements of progressive stability upon which we may restore the confidence of the nation and go forward with greater hopefulness than we have in the past. It is clear to everyone that the fear of danger cannot be overcome unless there are sound and substantial reasons upon which confidence can be based. Confidence cannot be established by well-sounding phrases, by Babbitt optimism. I repudiate with contempt, as I believe every hon. member of this house does, the fatuous and vaudevillian efforts of those who whistle to keep up the courage of the nation. They tell us to keep smiling and ask the penniless unemployed to buy more. They whistle these tunes at great public gatherings and try to get rid of the danger by their whistle. We cannot do that; we must have confidence but that confidence must be based on something substantial and real. It cannot be re-awakened by the hope of reintroducing a system now dead. There can be no resurrecting of dead institutions any more than there can be a resurrecting of dead bodies. The hope of Canada and the hope of civilization must rest in new performances, in new concepts, in new institutions and new practices. I believe that we are on the threshold of the greatest possibilities which time has ever presented to the human race.
The contributions of capitalism have been great, and one of its greatest contributions has been the abundance with which it has presented the human race. Capitalism has made it possible for us to emerge from the economic jungle where the tooth and claw method of survival was the order of the day and to reach a plane worthy to be called a real human plane. Prior to capitalism, humanity was in a state of perpetual scarcity, competition was the natural method adopted in the struggle for survival. But to-day we are in the age of plenty, as our subamendment very clearly outlines, and there is no more reason for a lack of bread, a lack of clothing, a lack of warmth, a lack of housing or a lack of any of the necessities of life than there is for a lack of water. We are

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
in the age of great surpluses. In one year Canada has produced a surplus of wheat sufficient for our needs for another year. If that were done in the case of all our products, the population of Canada would perish in a week unless we found better ways of distribution than have been found so far. The only method of distribution thus far discovered has been through the wages paid for production; if we produce a surplus there will be no more production, no wages will be paid and we will be faced with starvation in the midst of great abundance. The surpluses with which capitalism has presented the world may truly form the essential basis of cooperative economics. Those surpluses should be the basis of a higher system of ethics than humanity has ever been able to achieve in the past. We have tried to be ethical under a competitive system, but I say that we might just as well try to grow roses on an iceberg as to practise Christian ethics in the midst of a competitive civilization. Even ethics must have a satisfactory physical basis. With such abundance of all that is essential to life we are on the threshold of being released from economic bondage, the greatest bondage ever faced by the world. Before we can reach that freedom we must be prepared to remove all the restrictions introduced during the period of scarcity and evolve a definite method for the distribution of this abundance. This is a task beyond any individual, or even a government, it is a task for society as a whole. We must attempt to alter the whole course of society in order to reap the benefits of the great advantages which capitalism has presented to us.
To-day there is less cause for despair than at any other period in- history. At what period in history have human values received such universal emphasis as during the present period? Internationally there is a struggle going on for the establishment of a permanent basis for wrorld peace. Nationally there is a growing opinion that hunger and poverty are disgraces to society and we are seeking more and more to combine our human goodwill and intelligence in order to eradicate such as enemies of mankind. There is a growing opinion everywhere that the life and happiness of the people must not be hampered or denied by the limitations of certain agencies which man has devised to serve the purposes of life. Never were these human agencies so universal, so well organized, so articulate and potent as now. These qualities, together with our boundless national resources, or machine of production and our army of competent workers should be entered upon the ledger
of the nation by the Minister of Finance (Mr Rhodes) as assets of this country which no debts can outweigh.
We have a difficult problem to face, as have all people who have lived in similar periods of transition, but our assets are greater. Being heirs of the ages, we have greater knowledge to-day than ever before. Our knowledge is not only greater in the aggregate but the capacity of the individual is as great to-day- as, if not greater than, it ever was in the world's history. There is more goodwill in the world to-day than ever before, it has never been more general, more sincere and more forceful. We can still claim to be in possession of courage. Those who read of the exploits of our armies in Europe during the last war know that courage is still in the hearts of Canadians, and they will respond just as much to peaceful exploits as they did to warlike exploits. Human nature is on our side. When we talk about introducing a new economic system most people say: You cannot do that because human nature is against you. Human nature to some people is represented only by criminal exploits. But human nature is greater than that, it will assist us forward with our new system; it is one of the strongest forces in our favour. It is true that capitalism has developed much of the worst in human nature but if we can introduce a system such as is covered by our subamendment there will come a time when we will have an economic ss^stem which will bring out the best in mankind.
To-morrow we shall rediscover man himself and build a civilization worthy of his best. There are deeper wells of greatness in human nature than have so far been suspected. Then youth too is for a new system. The young people of Canada are looking for leadership. They are wise enough to sense the danger of the present system and to appreciate the instability which will come from the denying of the necessities of life in the midst of abundance. Finally that great force referred to by Schopenhauer, Goethe, and others as the "Will to live," has not lost its cunning, nor its creative genius. Having brought the race from the slime of incipient life to the highest achievements of modern civilization it wi'1 not now abandon us. It will discover what to do with abundance. The real challenge to capitalism does not come from communism or socialism, it comes from the will to live inherent in humanity. Capitalism must meet this challenge of life or perish. Life will not be defeated.
With such a heritage of power there is no room for fear, with such strivings of the vital
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

instincts of the race, civilization will and must oome through. Our despairs are but passing clouds before the vision of the mind. Our fears are like the dreams which waken children in the night. Such defeats as we fear may come to individuals, but the race is borne to victory. The great to-morrow is like an unborn babe in the womb of time. The sufferings of the moment, which are real and tragic, are the pains of birth. The life of -civilizations, like that of the race, must find its survival in -new birth. This truth I put down as the sure basis of hope. Beyond the happy scope of myth no corpse has ever come to life. Those who expect to resuscitate capitalistic civilization, like those who spend their times at graves in readiness to welcome resurrection, shall wear forever the dark mantle of despair. New thoughts, new ideals, new systems and new hopes are the new-born children of -to-day who shall be in command to-morrow.
I ask the house to consider the proposals which we put forward in connection with this anticipated new age of abundance so that we may be in a position to take advantage of it, and to vote for the subamendment and economic freedom for the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) upon his very interesting speech. I intend this afternoon to direct my humble remarks especially to my colleagues from western Canada, and I do not know amongst them a more amiable, lovable or sincere friend of the people than my hon. friend. Since I have come to this house, I have been much impressed by the assiduity of members from western Canada who sit with the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), by their spirit of cooperation and high sense of duty.
I did not intend to take part in this debate, but the very interesting speech delivered by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) has impressed me to such an extent that it behooves me, as a representative of an agricultural division of Quebec, to rise and thank him for having so happily voiced the sentiments of eastern Canada. The hon. member is still a young man; his political career is full of promise; his speech is one of the most persuasive that has been delivered during this session. My hon. friend has been an eloquent advocate of the needs of the farmers; being himself addicted to the farming and live stock industry, he speaks with authority, and I hope the government will avail themselves of the excellent suggestions

he has given them in order to promote the welfare of the farmers and thereby assure our return to prosperity.
May I also congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) upon his masterly achievement; his budget has been everywhere highly commended. The minister comes from the beautiful province of Nova Scotia which has been called by a humourist endowed with a high sense of reality: "The land of apples and statesmen." From that province also comes the distinguished financial critic of the Liberal opposition, the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). By a happy coincidence, they were both born in Amherst, and the brilliant city editor of the Montreal Standard wrote last Saturday in his paper, the following words:
There must have been something about the air of Amherst, Nova Scotia, that whetted minds in keenness and brilliance, in that it created two such outstanding Canadians:-
The hon. Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth.
It has been more or less the custom of parliamentarians to avail themselves of the opportunity offered by debates on the budget to praise the work of their respective parties. May I ask my colleagues, in these times of anxiety, to rise to higher ground and forget our party divisions and discussions? On the eve of the great Imperial conference which will, for the first time in history, sit in Ottawa, and which will have to enter upon the long-awaited agreements necessary to assure the economic revival of prosperity in the different dominions forming the British commonwealth of nations, I humbly suggest that we consider the salvation of our country in the light of our duty towards agriculture as outlined by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe.
Let us forget our divisions and recall the words used by Professor Leacock of McGill university in his recent book entitled Return to Prosperity, a book which will prove beneficial to all men interested in studying the different problems which will confront Canada at the Imperial conference. Professor Leacock on the first page of his book says:
"The Imperial conference meets on the call of an emergency."
Speaking in this house at a luncheon tendered him by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), the Right Hon. Winston Churchill said:
"Canada once again stands on the Yimy Ridge of the empire."
Another parliamentarian from England wrote the other day that all the delegates ought to come to Ottawa with outstretched hands.

The Budget-Mr. Gagnon
The Ottawa Citizen of March 5 had on the front page the following caption:
Preparing for Ottawa is Britain's new national slogan.
It continues:
Nothing has captured the imagination of the political, commercial and financial world like the great empire gathering which a few months hence assembles in the Canadian capital. Already ideas of the leading industrial, trade union and business organizations here have been collected by government experts so that a complete review can be made of Britain's trade position.
Have we forgotten our party divisions and discussions to reach such an equanimity, as to enable us to assure the success of that conference? Before setting our hearts to a task of such magnitude, must we not remember that we are Canadians and resolute to achieve a safe return to prosperity?
May I suggest that the imperative task which we must assume is that of safeguarding agriculture? Professor Leacock, in his book which I have just mentioned, calls agriculture "the sheet anchor of national safety." He says:
Agriculture is not a business; it is a way of living, a way of thinking. It carries with it elements of national life that no clattering shuttles and humming wheels can ever supply; in peace, comfort; in war, a guarding arm against starvation. England with a four weeks' parcel of food in August, 1914, ought to have learned this lesson once and for all.
Such a statement provides ample food for thought. Agriculture stands as the very foundation of a nation. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has rightly said that the "general progress of the dominion depends upon the success of agriculture and. . . upon the soundness of Canadian agriculture depends the future prosperity of this country." I endorse that eloquent sentiment. I regret, however, to say that eastern and western Canada seem to hold different views about agriculture; many people seem to forget that a western farmer as very different from his brother of eastern Canada. Western Canada has developed so rapidly during the last thirty years that the farmers of the west have a very moderate admiration for the fanners of eastern Canada. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that before sitting down at the table with the other delegates and devoting many long hours to a study and discussion of the economic proposals submitted by all the sister dominions of the British commonwealth, we should first of all see if our own house is in order. Let us ask ourselves whether eastern Canada rhoroughly understands western Canada, and 41761-140
whether western Canada thoroughly understands the east, which understanding must be brought about before we can have the frame of mind which is essential to building a strong national policy.
By the pact of confederation each province has been entrusted with the task of developing agriculture within its boundaries, and the Dominion government has seen to it that the farmers of Canada as a whole have been helped to stimulate Canadian trade at home and abroad and the production of Canadian commodities. Before the construction of the transcontinental railways and the opening up of new provinces in western Canada, the farmers of the east were not rich. They may not have been very progressive, but at least they were thrifty and paid their debts. In 1840 when the union of upper and lower Canada was brought about, lower Canada or Quebec-why should I not be permitted to say this along with many historians?-had no public debt, while upper Canada, or Ontario, had a large debt, which was paid ungrudgingly by the taxpayers of both provinces. Quebec was then more concerned about responsible government and the freedom of her language than with the hoarding of gold. The farmers of Quebec ever since have continued to be humble tillers of the soil. They have devoted themselves to mixed farming, and later, in the eighties, to dairying, which industry was really first organized in the province of Quebec. In this connection may I say that one of the fathers of the dairy industry in Quebec was a very respectable gentleman from Kamouraska, Mr. Edward Barnard, a brother-in-law of the Hon. Senator Ohapais, and the father of Mr. J. E. Barnard, the brilliant director of L'Evenement of Quebec. The farmers of Quebec have lived happily near the great St. Lawrence in the charming vales of the eastern townships, close to the grand Laurentian mountains, in their small, whitenpainted houses near the village church where they find the inspiration and the courage to carry on the work of their forefathers. At the present time the farmers of Quebec like the farmers of all Canada are suffering great distress, but nevertheless they cheerfully fulfil their tasks, and even now should any of my colleagues from the other provinces happen to be travelling along the St. Lawrence they will hear songs like Alouette, and other gay refrains coming from all the homes.
Confederation has brought to the farmers of Quebec new duties towards the other provinces which they have faithfully fulfilled. But the rapid development of western Canada

The Budget-Mr. Gagnon

and the building of railroads have changed the whole economic structure of this dominion. Thousands of emigrants have been induced to go to the western provinces at the expense of the public treasury. I remember that at the beginning of this century, when Laurier was defending his policy of immigration and was being criticized iby other parties on account of the disastrous consequences which might follow, that grand old man predicted in biblical language that the twentieth century would be Canada's century. A long procession of immigrants has followed the trail to the west, and millions and millions of dollars have been spent in building railroads and establishing those' immigrants on western lands. The crops of wheat of the Canadian west have become fabulous, so much so that Canada has gained the reputation of being the granary of the world.
Canada was then passing through a period of great prosperity and those who were criticizing the policy of the government oif the day in the matter of railroads and immigration were accused of being pessimists and of slandering their own country. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that every Canadian must be proud of our western provinces and of their splendid populations and of the courageous manner in which they have fought the depression, but I have no hesitation in submitting that the historians of the future will regret that the farmers of western Canada have been almost exclusively concerned in the extensive growing of wheat.
They were so successful in wheat farming, in real estate speculation and in other fields of speculation that they believed that prosperity would never cease, and sometimes they would throw a scornful look on the farmers of the east who, happily, remained backward. The western farmers have been so powerful in Ottawa that all parties have been begging for their support. Railways have been built for them in almost every district of Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and even during this session, Mr. Speaker, when we hear that our railroads, even the Canadian Pacific Railway, are on the verge of bankruptcy, hon. members from the west are urging the government to build a railway in the Peace river valley. Why, Mr. Speaker, should we not more frequently rise in this house and lay our cards openly on the table and say that, fortunately or otherwise, the ideals and customs and mentality of the Canadians of the western provinces are different from that of the east. Professor Leacock in the -book to which I have already referred makes a dis-

tinction that is worthy of consideration. He says at page 38:
There is in it an almost creative power that makes a British farmer, in the Greek sense, a poet. In Saskatchewan he is an engineer.
Is there not a good deal of truth, Mr. Speaker, in that contention? The farmers of the west are adventurous and bold engineers. The farmers of Ontario and Quebec are modest and thrifty tillers of the soil. In western Canada the farmers cultivate hundreds of acres of wheat. They raise hundreds of heads of cattle, have e^ich a great number of employees, and use the most modern machinery. The farmers of eastern Canada are not industrialists like their brothers of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, but they are nevertheless even more attached to the soil where they and their forefathers have been living for more than two hundred years.
Both the farmers of the east and of the west have contributed in their own way to the progress of this country. However, legislators have too often forgotten that the western farmers were engineers and industrialists and that the eastern farmers were different. If I may be permitted to refer to the Bankruptcy Act, which has permitted farmers to make an assignment of their assets for the benefit of their creditors, who will not now admit that while such legislation may have been suitable to the west it has proved disastrous to the farmers of eastern Canada. No farmer of eastern Canada ever at any time has demanded of the legislators that he be allowed to go into bankruptcy. I do not think traders and manufacturers have ever been less inclined than now to ask for such a remedy. I am sure that is the case, for in my eighteen years of practice before the bar never have I seen the estate of a farmer in bankruptcy pay one cent to the creditors. This is why it is that now in the province of Quebec societies of farmers, chambers of commerce, and members of parliament ask that the law be amended so that farmers be excluded from the jurisdiction of the Bankruptcy Act. Last week I appeared before the special committee of this house which is now considering a general revision of the Bankruptcy Act. Many prominent gentlemen from eastern Canada have appeared before that committee, among others, Mr. R. Messier, acting dominion secretary of the Retail Merchants' Association, Montreal; Mr. Lalonde, president of the Catholic Union of the Farmers of the province of Quebec, comprising 16,000 members; Mr. D'Arcy Leonard, representing the Dominion Mortgage and Investments

The Budget-Mr. Gagnon
Association, Toronto. At page 20 of the first report of the committee, Mr. G. T. Clarkson, the distinguished head of the firm of E. R. Clarkson and Company, who appeared before the committee to represent the Toronto Board of Trade and the Dominion Association of Chartered Accountants, said:
In my opinion a farmer should not be subject to this act.
The other day two prominent gentlemen, the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) and the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska (Mr. Girouard) moved each a resolution-which unfortunately has not been discussed-asking this government to take the necessary steps to exclude the farmers of Quebec from the jurisdiction of the Bankruptcy Act. Recently members from Ontario and Quebec have received a resolution from the Ontario Education Association asking the government to help reassure the credit of the farmers by excluding them from the operation of the act. Undoubtedly the Bankruptcy Act has ruined the credit of the farmers of Quebec.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I refer to other legislation which has been disastrous to the farmers of eastern Canada; I mean the law enacted in 1929 creating the Canadian Farm Loan Board. This legislation may have been beneficial to the western farmers, but it has not been at all helpful to the farmers of eastern Canada. The rate of interest is too high, the legal fees incident to the granting of loans are also, too high, and the obligation laid upon borrowers to contribute to the special fund is not only unpractical but absurd.
In a period of depression such as we are passing through at the present time we are in a good position to judge whether bankruptcy legislation or legislation for granting loans to farmers is practicable and suitable to the needs of those engaged in agriculture. I would suggest that all the laws concerning agriculture be studied, amended and readapted to suit the needs of the farmers of the different sections of the dominion. The hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) was right in his suggestion, that such a move ought not to be taken without consulting the provinces. It will be found that there is too much duplication in the granting of subsidies by federal and provincial governments, and such a situation tends to confusion and criticism. It seems to me that we ought to proceed by way of investigation. I was surprised last Sunday to read in the Montreal Standard that Premier Brownlee of Alberta wants a royal commission to be appointed to investi-41761-140J
gate agricultural conditions in western Canada. He is said to have declared that people in other parts of Canada, particularly in the east:
Were ignorant of the serious condition agriculture was in.
I will not say, Mr. Speaker, that the west is ignorant of conditions in the east, for such absolute statements are not at all conducive to harmony and cooperation between the east and the west, but I may summarize the views of the people of eastern Canada by stating that sometimes our western friends act as if they were ignorant of the problems which confront eastern 'Canada. Therefore it seems to me that it is necessary that we investigate agricultural conditions not only in western Canada but throughout the whole country. It does not seem to me to be necessary to have recourse to a royal commission now, but would it not be wise before the Imperial economic conference convenes for all the provinces to send delegates to Ottawa to submit their views with respect to agriculture, such as extension of credit to farmers, the best means of encouraging our live stock, dairy, maple sugar and beet sugar industries, and the sale of all agricultural products.
After the Imperial economic conference I would suggest that the government again invite delegates from all the provinces to meet in Ottawa to try once for all to settle their differences without having recourse to the courts. If we could give to our farmers all the money that has been spent to submit to the courts cases of conflict of federal and provincial jurisdiction, it would he possible to provide for them many beneficial measures of relief. At such a conference we ought to be able to meet in a friendly spirit, to place our cards on the table, and to be ready to make any reasonable compromises that may be necessary. And it would be well to discuss the advisability of giving back to the federal government the Quebec maritime fisheries that were in 1922 wrongfully given to the government of Quebec. This step is demanded by all the fishermen of Quebec, and is the only way to help the fishermen, as was admitted the other day by bon. gentlemen opposite, including the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. 'Casgrain) and the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff). We ought also to discuss the advisability of buying Labrador. It would be well, too, to discuss some practical scheme of credit for the farmers of eastern Canada. Finally, wre should take such steps as to remove all causes of friction between the provinces.
The Budget-Mr. Gagnon

But in the meantime the farmers of eastern Canada are facing an emergency and they cannot wait. Last year we helped the farmers of western Canada; now it is imperative to think of the east. Hon. gentlemen from western Canada, I ask you to help the farmers of eastern Canada. In this respect I do not know of any better scheme than that submitted so eloquently by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). He suggested that the government grant a bonus or subsidy to encourage the export of agricultural commodities. While we are passing through this economic crisis, stimulation to any avenue of development that will increase employment is surely highly justified, at least while direct relief is being paid out of the treasury. Australia is making a determined effort to sell more meats to Great Britain. May I support the contention of the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Belec) and ask the government to try to recapture the bacon export trade which we lost during the war. I think the government should impress upon the delegates at the Imperial conference that it is up to them to help Canadian farmers who, when they went abroad to defend the causes of liberty and civilization, had their avenues of trade in agricultural commodities taken by neutral countries such as Sweden, Norway and Denmark. Since the government are thinking of adopting a policy of direct relief for unemployment the door is wide open for the bonusing of exports of agricultural commodities, and I respectfully submit that such bonuses are necessary because of the present emergency. If we wish prosperity to return we must go to the rural districts and help the farmers create prosperity. Farmers are to save our economic system. Let us save the farmer and communism will vanish.
Let us try to understand each other, gentlemen from the west and gentlemen from the east. Our country is wonderful and we are proud to live in it. Let us secure the future happiness of our children. I respectfully ask my colleagues from western Canada to give us what we are entitled to, and to help our farmers since last year we helped save your western provinces from bankruptcy and ruin. If the French Canadian farmer, for one reason or another, would like to have two or three French words on Canadian bank notes and currency, should it not be a pleasure for our friends and brothers from western Canada to give such a token of courtesy to the four million French Canadians living in this country? With the great development in radio we have found a new way of exchanging ideas and opinions between all the provinces.

Let the old French Canadian romances be broadcast over the western provinces, and nothing will prevent cooperation among the different provinces, and the different races becoming closer and more intimate. In these times of sorrow and depression, if the government cannot give bread to all needy people, at least the government may satisfy the souls of the people.
May I close my few remarks by recalling the words of Right Hon. Winston Churchill, who said that "once more Canada stands on the Vimy Ridge of the empire." I think Vimy Ridge will always illustrate our history. The first time I saw the great painting which hangs on the wall of one of our committee rooms I was greatly impressed by the idea expressed by the painter. At the top of the hill stands a monument dedicated to our heroes by a grateful nation. From the foot of that historic ridge to the top the shades of our soldiers ascend, just as they did on the morning of that memorable day. There they died side by side, Mr. Speaker, brave English Canadians, sturdy Scotch Canadians, gallant Irish Canadians and indomitable French Canadians; there they died, and there their ashes are mingled. They died to give us peace, and now when we are all suffering let peace remain in our souls. Let us forget our differences, and our children will be proud of their fathers.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words in this debate may I be permitted at the outset to extend my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on the very able and concise way in which he presented his first budget to the House of Commons a few days ago. May I also extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) for the masterly way in which, as the official critic on this side of the house, he replied to the budget speech of the minister. Congratulations are also due to all hon. members who have taken part in the debate, and who have presented points of view pertaining to their own localities and their own interests. May I be pardoned if I do not follow very closely the remarks of the speakers who have preceded me; I desire to discuss a matter which is of some moment to us in the province of Manitoba and for which I may not have any other opportunity of discussing.
I hold in my hand extracts from a return brought down in the house some time ago showing the amount of money advanced by the federal government under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act to the governments of the four western provinces. It shows

The Budget-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
that as of February 26 there had been advanced to the province of British Columbia, $5,664,000; to the province of Alberta, $4,624,000; to the province of Manitoba, $3,205,000; and to the province of Saskatchewan, $16,302,000. It also shows that $6,500,000 was advanced to the province of Saskatchewan for purely provincial government expenses. I do not wish to infer in any sense that the province of Saskatchewan received more money or more federal assistance than it should have received, but I do maintain that the province of Saskatchewan is not five times worse off than is the province of Manitoba. When we see that the province of Saskatchewan was able to secure for purely provincial government purposes some $6,500,000 it does seem passing strange that the province of Manitoba could not obtain some assistance for the provincial savings office.
In his remarks on Tuesday last the Prime Minister stated in effect that it seemed rather hard that when he and his government were confronted with very trying conditions and faced with problems of great magnitude they should be the subject of abuse and a target for criticism. Well, Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman asked for the responsibility, and surely he will not deny anyone the right to criticize his actions. He usually defends his course with vigour and determination, but that is no reason why, if hon. members on this side of the house do not agree with what is being done, they should not have the right to criticize.
I wish now, Mr. Speaker, to refer to two editorials which appeared in Winnipeg newspapers some time ago. The first appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune, which is recognized as the Conservative newspaper in Manitoba, dealing with the closing of the provincial savings office. It is headed "Not Premier Bracken's Fault" and goes on to say:
Whatever other sins he may have to answer for. Premier Bracken cannot be justly saddled with responsibility for the downfall of the provincial savings bank. It is through no fault of his that the institution has been dismembered and its remains fed to the chartered banks.
Sir. Bracken stated his case in the legislature yesterday with moderation and restraint. It is worth noting by the way that a strong case needs no other kind of presentation. The facts speak for themselves without any accompaniment of sound and fury.
The facts speak for Premier Bracken in the circumstances of the constitution of the provincial savings bank and in the manner of its dissolution.
The last thing that was dreamed of or thought possible when the provincial bank was organized was that there could be such a thing as a public questioning of the safety of the deposits. The provincial savings bank was as
strong and secure as the province itself. There could be no danger to the deposits short of an upheaval that would put the province of Manitoba under the hammer in a sheriff's sale, a thing that did not happen, will not happen and could not happen.
But the unexpected thing and what seemed the impossible thing did actually happen. Depositors in the provincial savings bank became anxious about the safety of their money. Whisperings grew into street talk. Street talk grew into small withdrawals. Small withdrawals grew into quite general withdrawals. In short there was a run on the provincial savings bank which, continuing in rising intensity over a period of several weeks, absorbed most of the bank's ready cash.
There was an abundance of security behind every dollar of deposits-securities as good as the province of Manitoba itself-but these securities were not liquid in the chaotic market that prevailed. It became a question of the chartered banks advancing money on Manitoba's securities or the Dominion government advancing it. From neither source was the money available. The savings bank, strong in its foundations as the Rock of Gibraltar, had to go.
It has been said that if Premier Bracken had taken the public into his confidence and made a clear statement of the bank's position the withdrawal of deposits would have ceased. That is a bold conjecture.
If Mr. Bracken had publicly intimated that the bank lacked cash assets, but was otherwise sound the chances are that the run would have been intensified. He could only have made a public announcement with safety if he had been able to find the ready money support he was looking for, and invite all uneasy depositors to go to the bank and get their money. That was the only kind of statement to carry assurance to anxious depositors and stop the drain on deposits.
At no time was Premier Bracken in a position to make such a statement. A neighbourly spirit on the part of the Dominion government would have enabled him to do so, but the Dominion government was not in a mood to play that part. It remained a mildly interested spectator while the savings bank took the count.
From the Winnipeg Free Press I should like to read in part the following editorial:
Manitoba has lost an institution deeply rooted in the popular regard, as the fact that it had 40,000 patrons proves, under circumstances injurious to the credit of the province, and therefore detrimental to private interests as well. The disappearance of the bank is not a very favourable advertisement for Manitoba and Winnipeg. The banks, in keeping with the view that he who pays the piper has the right to call the tune, made their assistance, which was necessary to avoid a worse calamity, contingent upon the bank being turned over to them. They thereby removed what was to them a banking eyesore. The banks are not private institutions but public utilities; the propriety of the course which they have followed in this case, will be properly reviewable by the public when the facts are available.
It is known that the province applied to the Dominion government for help and met with refusal. The explanation by the Dominion, when it is made, may be completely satis-
2230	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. WeAr (Macdonald)
factory. In theory the Dominion is not responsible for Manitoba's financial enterprises; only the supreme consideration of the public safety could be invoked in an appeal such as that made by the province upon the Dominion. But if-as reports in Ottawa seem to indicate -Mr. Bennett, after denying the province, gave the banks aid in taking over the savings bank, the matter takes on a different complexion. But here judgment may well await the explanation promised by the Prime Minister.
Then there is the matter of the reported organized drive against the bank for ulterior purposes. Here there is something more than rumour to go upon. The premier of the province has said that the disappearance of the bank "must be charged in some degree to ill-considered gossip, but in considerable degree to deliberate propaganda." Deliberate propaganda! By whom and to what end? The people will expect further light upon this point.
Following the opening of the Manitoba legislature, which took place after the provincial savings office had closed, a member of the Labour party moved that a special committee of the house be appointed to inquire into the reasons for the closing of the savings office, and bearing directly upon the two editorials I have read, there are a few extracts of interest which I will read from the evidence taken before that special committee. The first extract I want to give is a report of the evidence of Mr. John McGregor, chairman of the board of trustees of the provincial savings bank:
Suspects Organized Campaign
"I suspect that there was an organized campaign behind it," said John McGregor, chairman of the trustees of the provincial savings office referring to the rumours that the institution was unsafe.
"They came out of the blue sky and were so persistent that one must believe they were organized. It is hard to credit any responsible person with doing that. There was no justification at all for these rumours."
The rumours came to the attention of the trustees on January 11, Mr. McGregor said, previously nothing definite had been heard.
Ill last October the provincial savings office was sound and prosperous, he said. The market value of the office's securities _ in April, 1931, revealed a balance of $377,000 in favour of the office, compared with the booked value. _
In September the value of the securities dropped precipitately, although the number of depositors increased steadily until the end of October. There were, however, unexpectedly heavy withdrawals in November, 1931, to purchase national service loan bonds.
At this point I may say that there was Withdrawn from the provincial savings bank in Manitoba, presumably for the purpose of buying national service loan bonds, the sum of approximately one and a quarter million dollars.
Mr. McGregor stated that the office had been liquid up to that time, although a credit of

$1,000,000 had been obtained from the banks as a precautionary measure against any drop in bond values.
E.	J. Jewers assured Mr. McGregor that there had been no great demand for deposits, hut shortly after January 11, Mr. Jewers informed him that the withdrawals -were becoming steady. A meeting of the trustees was called that afternoon and it was decided to advertise the soundness of the office to offset the rumours.
Royal Burrit, trustee, declared that political attacks on the financial position of the province were, indirectly, attacks on the provincial savings office. The condition of the office and of the province was closely related and any political speech prior to the closing belittling provincial financial affairs was also a blow at the office.
Great Britain's dropping from the gold standard seriously affected the position of the savings office, he stated. But all banks were likewise affected. The serious situation in the securities markets after Britain's action resulted in most banks being not actually liquid.
As a matter of fact, he continued, chartered banks to-day were permitted in their financial statements to value their bonds as of June, 1930, because at present bond prices none of them would be liquid.
The provincial savings office was the victim of circumstances, he continued. It was_ not at any time insolvent; only its liquid position was ever affected seriously and until the run its liquid position was sufficient to meet all depositors' demands.
Continuing with the evidence taken before that special committee, as reported in the press from day to day, I find the following:
Testifies Newton Advised Him To Withdraw Savings
Grandview Auto Dealer Tells of Conversation with Conservative Member for Roblin
F.	Y. Ne-wton, Conservative member for Roblin, in the first week of February advised a friend to withdraw whatever money he might have deposited in provincial savings office, a special legislative committee investigating the closing of the savings office was told Wednesday afternoon.
This testimony was taken from J. I. Orr, automobile dealer at Grandview, Man., who said he had talked with Mr. Newton in Roblin some time during the first week of February.
Before he named the Conservative member of the legislature, Mr. Orr said that a friend had told him that if he had any money in the provincial savings office, he should withdraw it. It was also suggested that Mr. Orr should advise any of his friends to withdraw their savings.	.
Questioned, Mr. Orr said that the friend who had given him the advice was Mr. Newton.
The next evidence taken before the committee is reported as follows:
Tell Of Warnings By F. Y. Newton To Take Out Savings
Schweitzer Also Quoted at Inquiry Into Provincial Savings Office
Prominent Conservatives early in February advised friends to close accounts in the pro-

The Budget-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
vincial savings office, witnesses Thursday told the special legislative committee investigating the closing of the savings office.
^ Two witnesses from Dauphin described how F. Y. Newton, Conservative member for Roblin, had warned that the institution was not Safe and advised them to take out their money and to tell their friends to close their accounts.
Val. E. Schweitzer, Conservative party organizer, told a friend that the savings office was "broke" and that he should withdraw his money another witness testified.
It was H. L. Pulford, a depositor in the provincial savings office, who said that the Conservative party organizer had advised him to close his account. Mr. Pulford was questioned by Hon. W. J. Major, attorney general.
The next evidence, dated . April 4, 1932, reads:
Willis Urged Brother To Withdraw Savings
Legislative Committee Probing Closing Hears of Wire From Member for Souris
Brief but decisive warning of the closing of the provincial savings office came to a depositor from a member of the Dominion parliament, it was revealed, Saturday, when the special legislative committee investigating the closing of the savings office resumed its inquiry.
This warning was contained in a telegram to Trevor Willis, and it came from his brother, Errick Willis, M.P. for Souris, who was in Ottawa. The telegram read:
"Withdraw money from Donald and Ellice."
This is the location of The Province of Manitoba Savings Office.
The committee also examined J. T. Haig, Conservative member for Winnipeg, question-i ng him to determine the source of rumours which had prompted the Conservative member to write to Premier John Bracken asking whether the provincial savings office was safe.
The coincidence that Mr. Haig's political speech in Brooklands, on February 15, had accurately, although stated interrogatively by Mr. Haig, revealed why Premier Bracken had summoned the legislature, was emphasized in the examination of the Conservative member.
Later on in the evidence Mr. Haig stated that he had communicated his uneasiness about the provincial savings office only to Premier Bracken and Colonel F. G. Taylor, leader of the Conservative party. When questioned as to whether he had discussed the position of the provincial savings office with anyone else, he said he had not. He then added that he might have talked to Dr H. C. Hodgson, president of the Manitoba Conservative Association.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) will pardon me if I do not join issue with him in regard to the subject which he has been discussing this afternoon. I came prepared to speak entirely on the Canadian National Railways. It would have been a great pleasure to have replied to the arguments presented by him in the house. After all, in respect to the savings bank of Manitoba, there are two outstanding facts: first, that the bank failed because of bad management on the part of the provincial government; second, that the Dominion government, by intervention, saved 42,000 depositors from, to say the least, a great deal of inconvenience and perhaps loss of money. Apart from that, I shall not say anything further. As lion, members are well aware, a provincial election in Manitoba is not very far distant when this issue will be fought out on the public platform of that province, and so far as we on this side are. concerned, we shall be glad to join in anj' such issue as this.
May I join with other members of the house who have preceded me in extending felicitations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on the very able manner in which he presented his budget and on the fact that during these difficult times he has been able to balance his budget?
With these few preliminary remarks I turn my attention to a discussion of what has again and again been stated to be one of the major problems facing Canada to-day. I could not understand the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) stating that the Canadian National railway system should be put into the hands of a receiver or sold to the

The Budget-Mr. Bowman
Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Surely a proposition of that kind cannot be supported.
I was very pleased indeed to hear the explanation made yesterday by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) with respect to a speech which he had previously made in this house, and as to the meaning of which there may have been some doubt. He stated that he was not in favour of any merger of the Canadian National Railway with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I followed very carefully the remarks of the hon. gentleman, previously made; I had read in full the speech which he delivered to the Canadian Club in Toronto on the Canadian National Railway, and I must say that I rather gathered from those two addresses that the hon. member did have in mind that the Canadian Pacific Railway might perhaps consider purchasing the Canadian National Railway. The reason I say that is that in his address at Toronto the hon. member made the statement that a purchaser might be found. Now when one thinks of any organization or corporation taking over an institution of the size and importance of the Canadian National Railway most people in this country would conclude that there is only one corporation in Canada that would be capable of doing it. I must say, however, that I do not think the hon. member for Stanstead gave his usual consideration to the proposition which he advanced in the house yesterday afternoon. As I understood that proposition it was this, that in all probability we would have to wait for a year before the royal commission on transportation would bring down its report, and that in the meantime the two companies be requested to pool their operations, whereby the hon. member thought a saving of eighty million dollars in one year might be made. May I point out to the hon. member for Stanstead just what that would mean? Calculating on the same basis as last year when economies accounted for a saving of 326,000,000 in the operation of the Canadian National Railways, 314,000,000 of which was in wages, to effect economies amounting to 380,000.000 would mean that between thirty and forty thousand railway employees -would have to be taken out of the service of the two railway companies immediately. That would be the result of following out the suggestion of the hon. member for Stanstead if the saving he suggests might be made were put into effect. I am sure that neither he nor any other member of this house would at this time suggest that thirty or forty, thousand more railway employees be thrown out of
employment without notice and without an opportunity to make preparation for the future.
In dealing with this question I purpose touching as briefly as possible on certain phases of the development of the Canadian National railway system, and of the problem as it exists to-day. All hon. members of the house are fully aware of the conditions under which the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial, the National Transcontinental, the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific were merged into one great corporation called the Canadian National railway system. I would draw attention to this fact, that at the time of that amalgamation, it was really a. merging together of bankrupt concerns. The Grand Trunk Pacific was in the hands of the receiver, the National Transcontinental was still in the hands of the government; the Canadian Northern Railway had failed in its ability to carry on during the war period and had secured financial backing from the provinces and federal government; the Intercolonial had shown deficits year after year, and the Grand Trunk had been dragged down to the verge of bankruptcy by the contract which it had made for the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific. It must be borne in mind that during those years of the merger, 1919, 1920, 1921, 1922, we were paying out immense sums to meet the deficits of these railways, as follows: 1919, $55,000,000; 1920, 380,000,000; 1921, 370,000,000; 1922,358,000,000. It must be borne in mind that at that time we had a medley of bankrupt concerns operating as separate and distinct entities, and operating at tremendous losses, with a great preponderance of main line mileage over branch line mileage, and with forty-one per cent of the roads out of the hands of the construction contractors only within the previous ten years. These railways were equipped as one might expect bankrupt concerns to be equipped. The first step for the new management of 1922-23 was to construct additional branch lines and to furnish the roads with proper equipment. To mention only a few of those items. Between 1923 and 1930 the following sums were spent; for branch lines, $65,000,000; permanent ways and structures, $106,000,000, of which $20,000,000 was spent in one item alone for creosoted ties; freight cars, $71,000,000; new passenger cars, $29,000,000; locomotives, $36,000,000; telegraph lines,, $7,000,000. One could go on giving similar sums which were spent in that way. It must be remembered when we speak of the tremendous sums of money which were put into these railways that we knew what kind of a bargain we were, making when we took them over. We
The Budget-Mr. Bowman

knew that large sums of money would have to be spent to enable the railways to operate as an efficient and economical unit.
I will admit that expenditures have been made which should not have been made. I do not think that there is anything to justify from fifty to one hundred million dollars being spent on terminals in the city of Montreal. I do not think there is anything to justify the tremendous sums of money that have been spent on the hotel system or on the triangular service on the west coast. The management of the Canadian National Railway undoubtedly made the same mistakes that other great institutions made. What great corporation during the boom years of 1927 and 1928 did not spend immense sums of money that should not have been spent? Nevertheless it must be borne in mind that during this period there has been built up a tremendously efficient transportation machine showing a vast improvement in the efficiency of labour, in mechanical power, in rolling stock and in every other department of railroading. This advance might be summed up by stating that in 1928 there was 31.5 per cent more traffic handled than in 1920 with 220 fewer locomotives and 3,370 fewer cars. It can be truly said that the Canadian National Railways can handle freight and passenger service as economically and as efficiently as any railway organization in the world. During this same period there has grown up among the employees an esprit de corps unexcelled in any similar institution on the face of the globe.
Now, with respect to these expenditures, might I point out that they are behind us, and that we have a well-equipped road ready to handle traffic as economically as any railroad on the American continent.
It devolved upon this new management to coordinate these roads into one great efficient transportation machine and to take every possible means to make the system pay. Just how far the management have succeeded in the performance of this duty under the circumstances which subsequently arose is perhaps a matter of diverse opinion. In times of depression like the present one is apt to stress, to the exclusion of everything else, the monetary loss and the tremendous sums of money from time to time put into this great enterprise. May I take the liberty of reminding hon. members of some of the obstacles with which the management have been faced. First of all, with respect to motor vehicle competition. The first year there were any registrations of motor vehicles was in 1907 when the number was 2,130; in 1910, 8,967; in 1915, 89,944; in 1920, 407,064; in 1921, 513,821;

in 1925, 728,005; and in 1930, 1,239,888-or in the last fifteen years between 1915 and 1930 an increase of 1,289 per cent. The first year that trucks were segregated in the registrations was in 1922, when 37,610 trucks were registered; in 1925, 74,489; in 1930, 165,464. In that same year the registrations of buses were 2,098.
Now, commensurate with this increase in the number of motor vehicles doing business in Canada, there has been an increase in highway mileage, until in 1930 we had 394,372-7 miles of highway, as compared with 42,075 miles of single line railway, 14,567 miles of second and third main track, industrial track, yard and sidings. I am quite free to admit that in the matter of short hauls at certain seasons of the year the motor truck certainly has an economic advantage over the railway. But may I point out that the competition as between the railways and the motor vehicles is most unfair, in that the railway companies are under the regulations of the Board of Railway Commissioners; their rates are fixed by the board; if they want to close a station they have to appeal to the board for approval; once passenger or freight service is established it cannot be changed without approval of the board, and so on all the way down the line. .There is no similar or analogous regulation in respect to motor transportation, and rates can be changed overnight. So we have this situation to-day, that the motor truck is carrying the freight upon which the railways charge a high rate and leaving to the railways the bulky and heavy freight such as grain, lumber and similar products. If this competition continues it simply means the whole rate structure of Canada will have to be changed. In the event of change it must be borne in mind that our grain cannot carry any higher transportation charges, otherwise it may mean considerable damage to our export trade. Then, too, railway employees have to undergo a severe medical examination to show they [DOT] are physically qualified to carry on their duties; no such analogous requirements are made of the drivers of motor trucks or buses. It must also be remembered that the railway companies as common carriers are liable for negligence, and as responsible parties they have to pay damages in the event of being held liable by our courts. Most of the operators of motor trucks and motor buses do not carry any insurance, and in many cases are owned by irresponsible parties, so that it is impossible to recover damages from them. And it must not be forgotten that the railway com-

The Budget-Mr. Bowman
panies operate upon their private right of way, constructed at their own cost, while motor transportation service is carried on on the public highway by corporations and persons operating for private gain.
These differences must be adjusted in fairness both to the railways and to the motor vehicles. I am satisfied that when that adjus-ment does come it will mean increased revenues for the railway companies. Not only so, but if by some coordination of the services a considerable portion of the motor business could be merged with the railway operations it would give employment to many railway employees who to-day are unable to earn a livelihood because of lack of work brought about by the shrinkage in railway traffic. In an article appearing in the March issue of Commerce of the Nation, under the heading "They Enjoy but Don't pay," Mr. A. D. Ferguson, of the bureau of economics of the Canadian National Railways, estimates that the reduced annual revenue of the railway companies of Canada through motor competition is $41,000,000, made up of $17,000,000 in passenger transport and $24,000,000 in freight transport. That was one obstacle to the success of the Canadian National Railway system.
Then, too, may I call the attention of the house to something else. It is generally conceded that in order to operate successfully and at a profit a railway company must have a gradual increase in traffic year after year. As hon. members are well aware, that has not been the case in Canada, though between 1923 and 1928 the revenues of the company have substantially increased. The figures are as follows:
