Surely the fact that the population of this country has not increased as was anticipated,
and that the business is not there to be done, cannot be blamed on the management.
Another obstacle to the profitable operation of this railway system has been the period of depression through which we are passing at the present time, but I do not know that this depression is without its blessings. With respect to the Canadian National system at least it has called to the attention of the country the seriousness of the problem with which we are faced, and I am sure hon. members of the house were gratified to learn that the estimate for capital requirements and deficit for the coming year has been fixed at some $71,000,000, or $41,000,000 less than the requirements for last year. I think the management are to be congratulated in setting up the finance committee and in making the economies which have been made. When the minister spoke on this subject he pointed out that economies last year amounted to some $13,000,000, and that for the coming year further economies would amount to an additional $15,000,000. In an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Globe shortly after the remarks of the minister on the tabling of the annual report of the company I find this paragraph:
The Globe sincerely congratulates the Minister of Railways on the needed economies which he has brought about-or rather which he insists that the management has brought about-in the operation of the National system. That the past period of prosperity and reckless rivalry in competition induced unwise and unwarranted expenditure is beyond question. Doctor Manion has given the country good service in insisting upon a return to sanity in enterprise and outlay. Retrenchment and rigorous economy-easy to preach but difficult to practise-must necessarily dominate the administration of the system for some years to come. Yet, at the same time, equally in the interests of the people who own the railway, there must be constant care that rigorous economy does not become crippling economy.
One would gather from the remarks of some hon. members that there was a vast difference in the results of the management of our two great railway systems. Let me quote from an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 6, 1932:
Canadian National railway operating revenues fell off in 1931 by $45,000,000. For the Canadian Paoific the corresponding figures are $40,000,000. Bearing in mind the difference of mileage and volume of business, the parallel is decidedly close. Operating costs were cut on the Canadian National $26,000,000, on the Canadian Pacific $27,000,000; freight reductions, Canadian National $31,087,127, Canadian Pacific $24,427,239: passenger reductions, Canadian National $8,439,816, Canadian Pacific $8,428,192. If there is any disparity in the earnings of the company in the final analysis, it pretty well resolves itself down into a question of density of traffic.
223S
The Budget-Mr. Bowman

The only remedy for our railway is more trade, more business, more population. All that the people of Canada can reasonably ask of the Canadian National management is that they should protect the property at the lowest possible cost to the public against the time when there will be a revival of prosperity.
The mention of economies naturally brings up the matter of railway employees, and coming as I do from a railway centre I must confess that when I hear of these tremendous reductions I feel that groups of railway employees scattered all over the country are bearing the burden of these economies. Today I received a letter from a man working in the shops at home. He has been employed there for some twenty-five or thirty years, and he tells me that the following reductions have been made in his salary in the last two years: First a day a week was taken off, which meant a reduction of $27 a month; then came the ten per cent reduction, amounting to $14 more and, within the last week or ten days he has been asked to take a further reduction of a day a week, which will amount to $27 more. This means that in the last two years his salary has been reduced by $68 a month. We should take these matters into consideration, and we should bear in mind that one of the invisible benefits to Canada from the operation of the Canadian National railway system is that last year there was paid in wages by the company the sum of $126,950,841, and that the average number of employees was some 91,416. Of every dollar spent by the railway company 63f cents went for labour, while 9 cents went for fuel This $126,000,000 spent in Canada means a tremendous purchasing power and a tremendous consumption, so the welfare of our railway employees is of vital importance to every citizen of this country. These employees have taken salary and time reductions, and some are out of employment entirely. In my own town there are men who have been with the system for fifteen or twenty years, in which time they have acquired seniority rights, nevertheless to-day they are unable to hold a job at all. They may work for two or three months in the course of a year. There is no more loyal body of employees to be found in any institution or corporation in the world than is to be found working for the Canadian National Railways to-day, and it does seem to me that considering their importance to Canada and the purchasing power they represent, together with the fact that with their dependents they number about 400,000 people, they should have greater representation on the board of directors of the company as well as on any other

board which has to do with hours of work, rates of pay and other related matters.
It must also' be borne in mind that during these years of efficiency in operation and economy in handling passenger and freight traffic, during this speeding-up process, the number of injuries to employees has increased to a remarkable extent. In 1915, the number of railway employees injured was 2,573; in 1920 it had increased to 7,719; in 1925 it was 8,256, and in 1929, 12,483. This is all the more reason why someone who is thoroughly familiar with the risks involved in the work should be on the boards which regulate the terms and hours of service.
There is another invisible benefit to Canada from the operation of the Canadian National railway system. I refer to the benefit that has resulted from colonization and settlement. I often think that this benefit is entirely overlooked. When the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) talks about handing the railway system over to a receiver, which I presume means the dissolution of the whole system, he should surely bear in mind that we .owe something to the maritime provinces in respect to the operation of the Intercolonial railway, and something to the remote districts that have been opened up and colonized through the operation of the Canadian National railway system. It should be remembered also that a vast amount of new wealth is being produced annually as a result of the settlement of those areas through the Canadian National Railways. In 1928, the Canadian National Railways handled, in grain products, 301,741 cars; live stock, 61,847; coal, 92,496; lumber, 112,459; pulpwood, 99,45S; pulp and paper, 61,654; other forest products^ 83,827. Most of these products have come from territory contiguous to the Canadian National railway system, and would not have been produced at all had not the system opened, up and given means of transportation to and from these various districts.

I take it from the
remarks of the hon. gentleman that he entirely disagrees with the observations of the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) and those of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi.

I have already covered
that.

My hon. friend has
skirted around the subject. Does he disagree with the remarks of those hon, gentlemen?

Surely the hon. member
heard me. I have made it quite clear that I

The Budget-Mr. Boulanger
disagree with every word said by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi.	*
And the hon. member for Stanstead?

And I have explained how far I disagree or agree with the hon. member for Stanstead. If there is one thing that can be said to clinch the argument for the continuance intact of the Canadian National Railways, it is the opinion expressed by certain members of this house and, recently, by Sir Henry Thornton before a committee of this house. At page 1644 of the 1932 Hansard, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) stated that had freight rates in Canada been the same as in the United States, $15,000,000 to $26,000,000 more would have been earned iby the railway company. And the hon. member for North Waterloo, at page 39S7 of Hansard of 1931, said that if the freight rates in Canada were as high as in the United States, the Canadian National Railways would not (be registering deficits but would be showing profits. Sir Plenry Thornton, speaking before a committee of this house recently, declared that Canadian rates were the lowest in the world and that, had the Canadian railways enjoyed the same rate scale as the United States roads since 1923, the Canadian National Railways would not only have been able to pay interest on all funded debt owed to the public, but would have had $20,000,000 over. Surely if there is anything to be said with regard to freight rates, so far as Canada and the United States are concerned, if population and density of traffic indicates anything, if -climate and terrain count, the facts are all in favour of a higher freight rate in Canada than in the United States.
Will the hon. member permit another question?
Order.
No; the hon. member knows I have only one minute left.
The hon. gentleman surely will allow me to ask this question. Is he in favour-
Order.
Is he in favour of the amalgamation of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways?
Absolutely no; not under any circumstances.
I think it would be the greatest calamity that ever befell Canada; it would be a government of railways and not government by this house.
Thanks for answering the question.

Thanks.
The Budget-Mr. Boulanger

session. I therefore extend to him my congratulations on his progress, and my best wishes that he may realize some day the goal of his ambitions. I would have been pleased to tell him that I entirely agree with the ideas he expressed a short while ago, as I also agree with those expressed in the house, a few days ago, by our friend the hon. member for Duf-ferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). The time has come for rural members of eastern Canada, representing the farmers of Quebec and Ontario, to agree in setting forth their claims in order to improve the lot of the farmers whom they represent in this house.
I wonder, sir, whether the Quebec farmers of whom I aim one of the humble representatives, may not be disappointed at the statement made in the house, the other day, by the hon. Postmaster General. During the 1930 election, our hon. friend posed as champion and guardian of his race and pledged himself, if elected, to be the mouthpiece of the farming class.
We therefore would have been pleased to hear him discuss the questions which interest specially the Canadian eastern farmers, and particularly those of the province of Quebec. We would have liked, for instance, to hear him speak on the policy the government intends to adopt with a view of opening up new markets to farm products; we would have been happy to hear him broach the subject of rural loans and state whether the government has the intention of lowering the rate of interest on these loans to farmers; and whether the government is to expedite and simplify the work of the commission on farm loans; we would have been delighted to listen to him discuss the subject of the tuberculins test and immunization of the dairy cattle; we would gladly have listened to him discourse on the return to the land movement and the .policy which the government may have as regards giving a tillage and land clearing bonus; we would have been pleased to hear the Postmaster General discuss the agricultural policy and the measures which the government has the intention of bringing down to improve the lot of this very industrious and important class in the social life of our country.
Instead of discussing these questions, the hon. Postmaster -General devoted the greater part of his speech to making excuses and apologizing for the government's fiasco.
The hon. Postmaster General had inured us to a more aggressive policy. During many years he was leader of the opposition in the Quebec legislature. I must admit that he performed this task in a creditable way. He was then somewhat looked upon as the representative and the mouthpiece of the Quebec

farmers; at least he delighted to -pass himself off as a country folk, as a farmer entirely devoted to the interest of the agricultural class. Judging by the speech he delivered the other night, and from which I shall quote a few extracts, I must say that he simply confined himself to offer excuses for the failure of the agricultural policy of the government. We would have -been -pleased to find out from the hon. Postmaster General whether the government has even an agricultural policy and whether it intends to really do something for the farmers. In reading over the hon. Postmaster General's speech, I discover, at page 2177 of Hansard, the following words:
The government cannot be held responsible for the present world wide crises.
A little further, in the same column, the hon. Postmaster General adds:
If prices of certain products are too low. the government cannot be blamed, but the fault is with the crisis prevailing all over Canada.

A guilty
conscience needs no -accuser.

Further on, in the same column he states:
Where is the country, which suffers less now from the crisis than we do?
On the following page we find:
If the result is not as great as could be expected, it is, I repeat it, due to causes of which the government is not responsible.
We have no responsible government!

At page 2179 of Hansard, the Postmaster General again apologizes for the government's inaction, in the following words:
There are many things which could be done under ordinary conditions, but we are up against hard times.
I want, sir, to contrast these few quotations taken from the speech delivered in the house, the other day, by the Postmaster General, with certain more emphatic statements which he made during the election of 1930.
We find one of these statements in an excellent newspaper, La Patrie, of Montreal, which is very sympathetic to the Conservative government and to the party-
Not at that time.

-and which has the reputation of being a well informed newspaper. According to this newspaper of July 4, 1930, the following is what he
states:
Will war be declared because I am elected as your member?

The Budget-Mr. Boulanger
May I here make a digression. The hon. Postmaster General and the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau)-neither of them is in his seat-charge us with having roused the passions and discussed conscription. If any one, during the 1930 election, discussed conscription and Canada's participation in the war, it is certainly these two hon. gentlemen.
In the same newspaper we find the following account of a meeting held at Laval des Rapides:
Mr. Sauve discusses the attitude taken by Mr. Lacombe in the house-
-the latter was his opponent-
-on various questions interesting especially, the farmers of his county and contrasts the indifference of the one who had just held the mandate with his own solicitude for the Quebec farmers.

Mr. A. Sauve addresses a meeting at l'Abord a Plouffe.	[DOT]

Farmers of Laval-Two-Mountains, did the policy which my opponent advocated in parliament bring prosperity and happiness in your homes? And you workmen who suffer from unemployment and whose wages are not in keeping with the cost of living, are you satisfied?
May I invite, sir, the hon. Postmaster General to repeat now these criticisms before the farmers and workmen of the county of Laval-Two Mountains. I would advise him to ask these farmers who sell their butter at 16J cents per pound delivered in Montreal, according to the market price ending April 16, 1932, whether they are satisfied. I would suggest to him to inquire from the civil servants whose salaries have just been cut, and especially those who have been dismissed, whether they are satisfied.

I have not been always successful, however, I have always stood by my guns because I am much attached to the people of my province; when it was a matter of championing the interests of the farmer, I was always present in the house.
Further on the newspaper says:
Then the speaker criticizes Mr. Lacombe for his attitude on farm loan, the rate of interest of which is too high considering the returns of the land.
I should have liked, the other night, to have heard the hon. Postmaster General re-41761-141

quest a reduction in the rate of interest on farm loans.

I shall go to Ottawa and I shall have sufficient courage to champion your cause under all circumstances. Are you, farmers, going to further submit to the competition of New Zealand butter, which is ruining you? And you, workmen are not your interests linked with those of farming, our main industry in Canada, because when agriculture suffers all are affected. After July 28, you will find in me both an energetic and fearless champion. ... I do not intend at the age of 55 to play the part of valet. If to-morrow . . .

-If to-morrow Mr. Bennett introduces a measure contrary to the interests of my race and my country, I will vote against it.
Did he introduce a single one?

Mr. William Tremblay, former member for Maisonneuve in the Quebec Legislature, was present at that meeting and, amplifying the remarks made by the hon. Postmaster General, he expressed himself as follows, according to the same newspaper:
Speaking on the lack of markets for wheat Mr. Tremblay stated that the government had failed in its duty because it had not come to the rescue. He spoke of the distress which resulted from such inaction. The whole of our economic life has thus been paralyzed, unemployment has gained ground and our purchasing power decreased.
On July TO, 1930, under the heading "A meeting held by Mr. Arthur Sauve at Oka" "La Patrie" reports the following words of Mr. Sauve:
Do you want as your member a man capable of rendering justice to both parties, Liberals as well as Conservatives? Do you want a man who remains pinned to his seat or a fearless man, capable of respectfully expressing his opinion and make known the requirements of his country and province?
May I point out to you, sir, that if there is a silent member of the cabinet, in the house, a minister pinned, bolted and padlocked to his seat, it is certainly the Postmaster General. He is not lavish with his words, he does not spoil us, he is rather- stingy in this respect, for, if my memory serves me right, the Postmaster General delivers but one speech each session.
On July 11, 1930, under the heading "I shall be an independent member free to protest when necessary" I find the following words in "La Patrie":
Farmers who bewail your lot, you whose children _ are disheartened and filled with anxiety, if you are content with such conditions, vote for Mr. Lacombe. But if you want protection, if is your duty to vote for me. The

The Budget-Mr. Boulanger
tariff policy of Mr. King is to blame for the conditions you complain of. The government pretended to change the tariff. But its policy is a deceitful one, to such an extent that the ministers avoid to discuss the results which the budget may have.
The last words could be applied to the hon. Postmaster General himself. When he spoke, the other evening, he was careful not to comment on the present budget he fought shy of the government's agriculture policy, which, in truth, does not exist. Continuing the Postmaster General stated:
If Mr. King is returned to power, I shall sit in the opposition free-as I claim in submitting my nomination-to support sound measures, regardless of party affiliation, such as duty will point out. I shall not be a member bolted to his seat. . . .
He insists on that expression.
. . . but I shall consider myself free to speak my mind when it pleases me and never seeking a reward. If I were aware that such a sacrifice would be expected from me, I would give up political life.
A senatorship.

I find
in "La Patrie's" issue of July 14, 1930. under the heading "Mr. Sauve answers Mr. Rinfret" at St. Placide, the following account of the hon. Postmaster General's speech:
Commenting on the crisis existing in this country, the speaker (Mr. Sauve), stated that the government must bear the responsibility of its policy. Answering Mr. Pouliot, the member for Temiseouata, who stated, a few days ago, that the low prices prevailing on butter were due to speculation, Mr. Sauve inquires why the government does not remedy such a situation and protect the farmers.
At St. Augustin, according to "La Patrie" in its issue of July IS, 1930, Mr. Sauve refers to rural questions in the following terms:
Mr. Sauve endorses the policy of a full indemnity for full bred or crossed cattle slaughtered by government officials pursuant to their tuberculine test policy. However, he prefers that, previous to having recourse to such means, immunization should be resorted to, in other words that cattle be treated instead of slaughtered immediately.
We should have been delighted to hear the hon. Postmaster General, who posed as the champion and guardian of the interests of farmers, in the 1930 election, discuss, in the house, the tuberculine test and immunization question of cattle, however he took great care not to do so. At the St. Eustache meeting, on July 20, 1930, our hon. friend broached the subject of Canada's participation in the Empire's wars, and pledged himself not to be the accomplice or the enemy of his race,

neither at Ottawa nor anywhere else. The report of this speech fills two or three columns; I shall not take up the time of the house to read it, but I shall add that after these pacifist statements of our hon. friend the platform collapsed. That topped the climax.
I closely followed, the other evening the speech of the hon. Postmaster General and I wondered what excuses the government could invoke for its negligence towards the Quebec farmers; I wondered what reasons they could give for the indifference they show towards the interests of the farming classes in Canada, had they not the Quebec government and Mr. Tasehereau to fall back upon. Our hon. friend the Postmaster General, with his inoffensive and kind look is a cunning gentleman, he knows how to change the subject in order to avoid an embarrassing question or to turn a difficulty; he thus endeavours to change the discussion to the Prime Minister of Quebec and the latter's government.
I closely followed the excuses he made so as to avoid making a frank and clear statement with reference to a bonus on butter and farm products exports. To my mind, the excuse made by the hon. Postmaster General is quite a childish one. If it is a sound measure, it is so independently of the views of the Hon. Mr. Tasehereau or his Minister of Agriculture. However, I listened to the hon. Postmaster General state, the other evening, with much candour: "If we do not grant an export bonus on butter and other farm products, it is because Quebec has not requested it, it is because the Quebec Prime Minister and his Minister of Agriculture opposed this measure."
First, this statement must be substantiated. However, were it true, since when does this government await, in order to act, that the Quebec government communicate its policy; since when does this government await, in order to introduce a measure, that the Quebec government requests it or any other provincial government? If this bonus is in the interest of farmers, not only of Quebec but of the whole of Canada, this government should itself take the lead in introducing such legislation without waiting for a request from outside. It is, moreover, the first time that I hear a member of the Dominion government state that their policy on a question which interests Canada depends upon the wishes or views of a provincial government.
The hon. member also referred to his statement during the 1931 provincial election with reference to the bonus on butter exports. He contends that he simply stated that the Dominion government would readily consider the question should the Quebec government

Supply-Secretary oj State
make such a request. Well, sir, let me inform the Postmaster General that what is needed at present, what the eastern farmers and those I represent request are not tedious speeches but action. Moreover, the minister was more emphatic in 1931, in the course of his campaign than he was, in the house, the other evening. As evidence, I shall quote a statement he made at a meeting held at St. Eustache, as reported by "La Patrie," in its issue of August 10, 1931, under the heading "Mr. Jean-Paul Sauve promises an inquiry in connection with the Beauharnois Water Power Company."
Hon. Mr. Sauve: When the famous butter question came up, the Bennett Government decided to put an end to this avalanche of New Zealand butter. If the low prices on butter still prevail to-day the Liberal government is to blame. The moment our government assumed power, it cancelled the New Zealand treaty. We promised a bonus on butter, we shall keep our word. The Liberals contend that this measure is absurd. If the Conservatives win the election in Quebec, you may rest assured that you will have it. I am aware that Mr. Bennett" favours such a policy as does Mr. Camillien Houde.
I suppose that there were at the meeting sceptical people who, having heard, in 1930, the pledges of the Postmaster General, had their doubts about the new promises, which were now made in 1931 by the hon. Postmaster General, so turning towards these sceptics, he said:
Remember that it was a Conservative government which, the first, granted a bonus on all Canada's exports.

Item agreed to.
Public Archives-salaries, $90,630; contingencies, $13,500.

There is a
very substantial reduction. Is the staff in the archives being cut?

The late Doctor Adam
Shortt, who held an important position in the archives in a consulting capacity, and wTho received a very considerable salary, was removed by death during the year, and we have not as yet filled the position. In addition, Mr. Smith, who was the assistant deputy archivist, has also died, and we are not at present filling his position. There have been a number of minor changes. There are two clerks, grade 2, whose positions we are not filling for the present; also the position of secretary to the executive in the archives, and a departmental librarian. These have all been removed by death or by reaching the age for retirement. I thought in view of the existing conditions and the ability of the present staff to carry on, it was expedient not to fill these positions for the present, and that has led to a considerable reduction in the appropriation.

I presume that the minister appreciates as we all do the importance of the work of the public archives. It would be very undesirable that it should be neglected in any way, as it is one of the most necessary works to be carried on under the government.

So far as the work of the
Archives branch is concerned it will be carried on with full efficiency, but the publications which we have been putting out from time to time may be delayed for a year.
May I ask if anyone is carrying out the special work upon which Doctor Shortt was supposed to be engaged for the last few years?

For the last few years
Doctor Shortt was engaged in compiling an index to certain important documents which had been acquired in England for the archives.

That work was pretty well completed. As a matter of fact, a year ago I would have retired Dr. Shortt except that for a considerable number of years he had been a very efficient employee of the government and had rendered great service to Canada, and I thought that under those circumstances I should keep him on until he asked to be retired. Less than a week before he died I had a conversation with him, and he told me that he would like to remain on for another year, although he had reached the age limit. I was very sympathetic to his request, and had an order in council passed extending his time for a year beyond the age limit; but he passed away very suddenly.

What is the age limit?
Mr. CAHAN; Seventy.

Would it not be desirable
to pursue the same policy with regard to the other officials of the archives?-because there are very few men who have been trained to do that kind of work.
Mr. 'CAHAN: Those connected with the archives who have reached the age limit, so far as possible I have kept in their present positions. The Dominion Archivist, Doctor Doughty, has given long service, and since I have been administering this department I have secured two extensions of time for him because he is known to be very efficient indeed. The time will come, of course, when new appointments must be made. My own personal opinion is that we can eventually secure the services of some one, possibly not as efficient as Doctor Doughty, to deal with the matter of maintaining the archives. Really what the department will require is an efficient financial administrator, who should have about him men with technical and expert experience in the matter of archives.
There are, I believe, a large number of university men doing research work in the archives. Will the cutting down of the library staff make it more difficult for them to carry on their work?

Not in the slightest degree. Each one who comes from a university to make investigation at the archives is given a separate desk, and there are all the clerical conveniences necessary for assistance in the work. That is not diminished in any way.

Secretary of State-salaries, $316,818; contingencies, $68,280.

Is there any particular item in the minister's depart-

Supply-Secretary oj State
ment on which we may discuss war reparation claims?

Yes. I am bringing down a supplementary estimate, as is customary each }rear, for payment of reparation claims, and that will afford full opportunity for discussion of the subject. It is on that item that discussion has taken place in previous years.

Is any action contemplated by the minister's department to maintain better control over the issuing of charters to corporations to see that the capitalization of the companies bears some relation to the real assets behind them?

Since I have been administering the department, close supervision has been exercised over the granting of charters, and I have not received or heard any complaints since I undertook its administration. Every charter is carefully examined, and large powers which were previously given to companies are no longer granted.
Can the minister give any indication as to when the supplementary estimates will be down with regard to reparations?

I would suggest that the Minister of Finance answer that question. I have put in my estimates to him, and I think just as soon as we complete certain business now before the house they will be brought down.

In his statement the minister led the committee to infer that the charters now issued were subject to some restrictions in comparison with the old charter forms. What is there in the new charter forms that was not in the old type granted toy the department?

Perhaps the hon. gentleman is misconstruing my remarks. I said we have made strict personal supervision of all applications for charters, and have dealt with them on their merits. Our object has been to restrict the charters granted on these applications to those powers which are really essential for carrying on the business contemplated by the applicants.
Mr. Chairman, the minister distinctly said in his first statement that the powers granted now were not as wide as those formerly granted. I am anxious to find out what powers have been withheld.

If the hon. gentleman would put his question in a different form I could
answer it; I cannot answer that general question. All I say is that every application for a charter is examined and investigated very strictly, and if the applicants seek powers beyond what we deem necessary for the purpose of carrying on the business contemplated, we restrict the powers granted very much indeed as compared with the practice in former years. That is a matter of personal supervision and investigation dealing with each individual application as it comes in.

I am
anxious to find out what difference there is to-day in the granting of these charters. The minister distinctly said that the charters granted to-day do not have as wide powers as was the case formerly. What did he mean by the "large powers" formerly granted that are not granted to-day?

I thought I had explained
it three times. If the hon. gentleman is accustomed to dealing with powers granted to companies I think he will easily perceive what is meant. In order to answer his question I would have to take each application that has been before me since August, 1930, deal with that application on its merits, and show what powers were applied for and what granted. [DOT]
Not at all; just give us one illustration.
I see in some cases there has been an increase. How is the total decrease of $53,000 odd arrived at?

If the hon. gentleman will look at page 96 of the estimates giving the details, he will see that formerly we had one head clerk receiving a salary of $3,000 ana one departmental librarian receiving a salary of $2,800; we have not filled those vacancies. Then at the foot of the page he will find the messenger service has been reduced, and that an allowance formerly given to the private secretary has been discontinued. The savings are represented by small amounts of that nature. We have refrained from filling vacancies which have occurred in order that we might keep down the gross amount of the appropriation. I have done what one would do in his own business.

For years past
there has been-shall I say?-a tendency to make it rather difficult for aliens to become naturalized. During the depression a great many newcomers to this country have found themselves discriminated against; they are often the first to be turned off work, and in some instances pressure has been put upon the immigration department by municipalities
Supply-Secretary of State

to have them deported. I should like to have the Secretary of State make a statement with regard to the policy of his department in affording opportunities for these immigrants to obtain their naturalization papers.

In 1930, the first year I was in office, there were 10,906 certificates actually issued; in 1931 there were 14,790 certificates issued; so the statistics would indicate that we have not put the restrictions upon the number of certificates issued which many people in this country think we should place. As a matter of fact applications for naturalization are made to the county court of the district in which the applicant resides. If the court refuses to recommend the granting of the certificates, under the law there is no option allowed the Secretary of State to issue the certificates. In some cases, in which I have thought the full evidence was not heard or that due weight had not been given the evidence given before the county court judge, I have asked the under-secretary of state to refer the case back for rehearing in order that injustice might not be done. Apart from that, since I have been in office, after receiving the report of the county court judge ' we have made independent inquiry through officials, as far as we could, in order that we might test the character and standing of the applicant in his community. So many applications have been made that I have been told-though I have no accurate information- that in some instances the county court judge has heard forty or fifty applications in an hour, which would mean that it would be almost impossible in that time for him to make due inquiry. Where mistakes have arisen we have endeavoured to investigate very sympathetically, yet very carefully, in the hope of providing that injustice should not be done. I cannot say very much more in answer to the question of the hon. gentleman?

I was just going to ask a question along the same line, though perhaps from a different angle. During last summer, and especially in the months of July, August and September, I noticed that the number of certificates issued ran from 2,000 to 4,000 per month. I was going to ask the minister if in his opinion these increased numbers were due in part to the hard times through which we were passing and to the possibility that in regard to employment or to the obtaining of relief those naturalized citizens had a preference, and that consequently there was a greater rush than usual on the part of people who desired to become naturalized. I wonder if the minister could
'Mr. Woods worth.]
say whether that was one of the reasons for the increase during those months.

It is quite possible that this may have been one of the reasons, but to us in the department it seemed that one of the chief reasons for the increase was the adoption of the old age pension act by so many of the provinces. In the west, from which my hon. friend comes, it appears from the applications that settlers who have been in that country for ten, fifteen or twenty years without applying for naturalization, have been told on application for a pension that a pension could not be granted except through the production of a naturalization certificate. I think that has been one great incentive, especially in the provinces of the middle west.

There is one other
question I should like to ask the minister, in connection with the explanation he gave with regard to the somewhat restricted powers granted companies applying for charters. I gathered the impression-and I wanted to make sure that my understanding was correct -that a company applying for a charter for the erection of a smelter, a saw mill, or something of 'the kind, would be held strictly to that undertaking. In the old days the powers granted were so wide in their terms that under such a charter the company might not only erect a saw mill or smelter but might build a railway, establish a line of steamships, obtain various concessions, in fact carry on almost any activity which might be desired. I understand that at present the minister is taking care that the powers granted are restricted to the one object in the mind of the company. Is that so?
Mr. CA'HAN:	As nearly as possible. In
reply to the other question I would direct the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that during the last two years throughout Canada an effort has been made to induce aliens resident in this country to apply for certificates of naturalization. I have noticed newspaper reports to the effect that hundreds of sermons have been delivered by clergymen, especially those of the United Church of Canada, advising their parishioners, who are aliens, to apply for these certificates. In the east there are certain associations, such as the Kiwanis clubs and others, who have been carrying on a great deal of propaganda along that line from day to day, and I am sure those educational efforts have induced a great many to apply for naturalization who had been negligent in not doing so previously.

Supply-Secretary of State

I did not quite make
myself clear. The second question I asked had no relation to naturalization certificates; I asked if my understanding of the minister's statement with regard to the narrowing down of the powers granted to companies was correct.

I thought I answered that.
We try to keep them limited to the objects they really have in view.

I should like to know whether any steps are taken to see that the capitalization allowed these companies will not permit them to issue a large amount of watered stock. I have in mind some very unfortunate cases in Canada, of companies incorporated under dominion charters which issued a great amount of watered stock that in some cases was held by our life insurance companies, and which proved to be almost worthless. I should like to know if the minister can assure the house that action is being taken by his department at this time to see that the capitalization of many of these companies applying for charters is not such as to permit them to issue watered stock.

I can only say that we do
examine these applications strictly, and we endeavour to keep the capitalization within reasonable limits. But after many years of experience in the organization of companies, from the legal point of view I must tell the hon. gentleman that as yet I have never seen a restriction on stock issues that I could not find a very effective and legal way through or around. Mere statutory enactments are very inefficient in that respect.

The minister, speaking
from his experience, said that it was impossible to restrain companies from issuing watered stock. Does he mean that the department of the Secretary of State is impotent to control such matters?

The Department of State
carries out the law by careful investigation and supervision. Outside of that the department has really no authority; it does not make the law. My suggestion to the hon. gentleman was that what is necessary is to see that no large powers are given in that respect under the law. Nevertheless, those who are astute in such matters can circumvent the law very readily.

In view of the further
answer the minister has given, to the effect that so far as the present law is concerned it does not give his department power to control
the capitalization of these companies, has the minister given any consideration to the possibility of amending the Companies Act so that that power shall be in 'the hands of the Secretary of State, to see .to it that no watered stock shall be issued as has been done in the past? Is that contemplated?

If you will allow me to
make an egotistical answer, were I to continue for the next half century as Secretary of State, I might do that while I could administer the act; but I do not think I could frame an act which would govern the conduct of my successor.
Carried.

I hope hon. gentlemen will nott try to rush this matter without giving it proper consideration. If that is what they intend to do, we can retaliate, although we do not wish to do that. Would it be possible for the minister to devise ways and means at least to curb the situation to some extent? The minister must be aware of what has happened in the last few years, and more particularly during the prosperous period. Many companies split their stock, no new capital being put in, and the people have to pay such commodity prices as will return dividends on that watered stock. Surely the minister is not so impotent in this respect that he cannot propose ways and means of curbing the situation.

I know of no way of curbing the gullibility of the small Canadian investor. If he will carefully examine the stock offerings made to him, I am sure he can put an end to that riotous dealing in stocks to which the hon. gentleman has referred.

But surely
the minister does not intend to say that it cannot be Stopped. Reputable firms in the past have gone out and sold watered stocks and ruined the purchasers of such stocks, and are we to sit by and say that we are utterly impotent to put an end to that sort of thing?

The very fact that so many are sent to gaol and to penitentiary for long terms shows that the law is being enforced at the present time. The enforcement of the law with respect to civil obligations is not, however, a matter for my department or for the government of Canada; it is a matter which is imposed by provincial law and within provincial jurisdiction. All I can do is to supervise carefully each charter granted in order to see that, so far as human foresight can foresee, these powers are limited so that
Supply-Secretary oj State

they cannot be used for fraudulent or illegal purposes.

Yes. But
my hon. friend will readily understand that notwithstanding anything the provinces may dp by setting up boards or commissions to investigate companies and to investigate the issuing of stock and its sale in the provinces, along comes a dominion charter covering all the provinces and providing no control at all. And these are the charters that are exploited all over Canada.

My hon. friend's opinion is
not in accordance with the view of the privy council, which says that dominion companies in the respect he mentions are controlled by the provincial authority and are under provincial jurisdiction. My hon. friend should carefully consider it. If he does, I think he will find that the charters which are now being granted are granted under, I do not like to say more careful supervision-I am not making any reflection on my predecessor- but under the supervision of one who has had, as I have had, an experience of thirty or forty years with company law. That experience enables me to assist the officials of the department in imposing restrictions which are beneficial and advantageous to the public. For instance, we found that dominion companies which had acquired surpluses weie selling out and then organizing again under practically the same names to carry on the same business, after having denuded the treasuries of such companies of a large part of their liquid assets. That sort of thing is not carried on now because that sort of company cannot secure a charter from the department under present conditions. I have no control over provincial jurisdictions. Not long ago a member of this house brought to my attention a certain company which had reorganized, and said that they had issued a lot of stock, watered and all that sort of thing, and blamed me for not exercising proper supervision. What I found was that the applicants for that charter had come to our department and, having failed to secure the wide powers which they had applied for, they simply went to a provincial secretary and secured from that provincial secretary's office all the wide powers which we had refused.
Carried.

I do not know why these gentlemen to the right are so anxious to rush this thing through. In the meantime some of us want to learn more about it. First of all, I should like to know this. After

a charter is granted, what reports are made by the company to the department? Secondly, what supervision has the department over such companies?

Every company makes an annual return of its affairs to the department, and that is examined in the department and kept on file for inspection by the public. Outside of that, with regard to their operations, we have no supervision and control beyond seeing that the law is complied with in the respects I have mentioned.

I want to say a
word in support of the position taken by the hon. member for Acadia. Everyone, I think, must realize that there has been a great deal of fleecing of the public not merely by speculation in stocks, about which we have heard, but by the process known as the watering of stock, and I do not think things should be left in the hands of the minister in this regard. It seems to me there ought to be legislation. We may have competent ministers and less competent ministers, conscientious ministers and less conscientious ministers; but we ought not to depend upon the individual. Surely there should be some sort of legislation which would protect the public. The minister has said that you cannot protect people who are gullible. That is not quite fair to the public. The fact is that company operations and manipulations have become so complicated to-day that the ordinary man cannot begin to follow them. And there are a great many legal gentlemen in this chamber who perhaps do not follow them very closely, because when a particular matter comes under scrutiny-as for example, Beauharnois-we have endless controversy as to just where each party stands and what is the real situation. Under these circumstances it seems to me that there should be some sort of law which would protect the public.
May I give a simple illustration? If a milkman coming into town stops at a pump and fills his cans half full with water, he is liable to prosecution. We say he is selling watered milk, an inferior article. I suppose it is something like that we have in mind when we say that a stock is watered; yet the minister seems to be taking the ground that while the public can be protected from unscrupulous milkmen, it is impossible to give protection against unscrupulous promoters or manipulators of company stocks. I do not think we can properly take that position. Incorporation is a great privilege; it affords protection to a company, gives it a standing in the community and enables it to enjoy a certain confidence which otherwise would

Supply-Secretary oj State
not be reposed in it. Incorporation gives a company the right to transact business under certain conditions, and it seems to me that having those special rights and privileges conferred upon it, it should be under some sort of state supervision. I know the character of the reports which come in; I remember once or twice having to look up some of them, and I found they were of a perfunctory character; they did not go sufficiently into the business of the company to enable the minister and his officials to know just what the company had been doing and what its standing was at the moment. It may be that this would require much supervision, as in the case of insurance and loan companies; it might involve considerable expense, but if the companies receive incorporation they might be charged such fees as would ensure their being properly supervised.
I ask, as the hon. member for Acadia has asked: Is it not possible to bring before this house legislation which would do more than is being done to-day in the way of safeguarding the public interest? I do not think I need say to the Secretary of State that the public feels very keenly with regard to this matter. An effort has been made in at least some provinces to control companies in the interests of the public, and something of that kind should be done here.

There are laws which visit heavy penalties upon those who water or otherwise deal fraudulently with stocks. The same process of law which indicts and commits to gaol or punishes by both fine and imprisonment those who water milk, brings to the bar and possibly to the penitentiary those who illegally or fraudulently deal with stocks. Under section 120 of the Companies Act wide powers are vested in the Secretary of State, but they can be exercised only on complaint. For the first time in the history of this country I have brought this section into effective operation. No application has been made under that section without a complete and thorough investigation being made, and at times there have been exposures of dominion companies who were dealing fraudulently with their stock, their shareholders, or the general public.

I am not reflecting in any way upon the Secretary of State, but I would point out to him that while it is comparatively easy to secure a conviction against a milkman, it is very difficult for a man who has a few shares in a great corporation to set in motion the wheels which will 'bring the big culprit to justice.
In that I differ entirely from the hon. gentleman. His statement simply shows the great abyss which exists between his attitude towards the administration of the law and my own.

In replying to my previous question, the minister evidently did not get my point. He made the statement that his department was doing everything in its power to see to it that the small investor was protected and that any company violating the law was brought to justice. I have before me a publication which shows the investments of the Sun Life Assurance Company-
The Sun Life Assurance Company does not come under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State.

I find that that company has invested in Imperial Oil Company Limited, stock to the exent of 655,500 shares, at a purchase valuation of $7,672,276.78. The present valuation of these shares is given at $5,244,000, showing a net loss to the Sun Life company of $2,428,276.78. The Secretary of State must know that a few years ago the Imperial Oil company split its shares four to one. What has the minister done with that company in regard to that question? Did he take any action? Would he take any action with respect to any company which followed that same course to-day?
The matter of the Imperial Oil Company has not been brought to my notice.
I bring it to the minister's notice now.
I see no reason in the world, morally, legally or otherwise, why a company with shares valued at $100 should not split them into four shares valued at $25.
The minister is begging the question.

I am not begging the question, I am looking it straight in the face. Furthermore, I say to the hon. gentleman that if he will take the stocks and bonds outstanding in this country, dominion, provincial, municipal, town and county debentures and the stocks of the various companies as they were valued in 1929, he will find that to-day the average value of these bonds and stocks is as 35 is to 100. There has been a tremendous loss, amounting to millions and tens of millions of dollars, in the value of the stocks of companies which have been honestly
Supply-Secretary of State

and efficiently administered. That depreciation in the value of these securities is not due to the splitting of shares nor is it solely due to the manipulations which have occurred in the stock market.

The reply of the Secretary of State is simply 'begging the question. The minister has made the statement that because of the decrease in the value of stocks, the weighted value to-day is only 35 as compared with 100 previously. I ask the minister this question: Suppose the Imperial Oil Company had split its stock four to one and had not put in any new capital; suppose the International Nickel company had split its stock without putting in any new capital, had those stocks not been watered would they not have been worth more on the market to-day than they were worth before that action was taken?
The hon. gentleman is under an entire misapprehension with regard to watering. Take the Canadian Pacific Railway Company-
That is a different thing.

In that instance one hundred dollars of stock represented over $100 of cash invested; 'tihe shares were split four to one and the par value of the present share is $25. Unfortunately it is selling on the market for less than that, but there is no watering in that transaction.

The minister has put
up a big straw man and has knocked him down; that is all he has done. We know quite well what the Canadian Pacific did; they did exactly what the minister stated they did; that is to say, they took a S100 share and split it into four $25 shares. That is the face value of Canadian Pacific stock to-day. Their excuse, when itheir bill was before the railway committee for its endorsation, was that they wanted small investors in Canada to participate in buying Canadian Pacific stock in order that more would be held in this country rather than ouitside it. But to how many companies does that apply? The minister has mentioned the one company we know of, but what about the other companies: what about International Nickel, the Massey-Harris and all those other companies that have split their stocks without putting any more capital into them and have not split their Stocks in the way the minister has cited the Canadian Pacific as having done? The minister is sidestepping the issue, and so far as I can see he is not willing 'to tackle the problem as the people expect him to tackle it.

I wish
simply most respectfully to suggest to the minister thait .this matter is really worthy of his serious consideration. Only the other day, in the special committee on radio broadcasting, Mr. Beatty, president of the company to which the minister has referred, proposed the creation .of a great private broadcasting corporation for Canada and suggested that the stock of that company might be held by various individuals and interests within the country, subject to certain restrictions. One condition he mentioned was that the stock should always be held by and be transferable only to Canadians, this Obviously being in order to maintain Canadian ownership. So Mr. Beatty was asked whether he would take any exception to the inclusion in the charter of a clause that would prohibit at any time in the future the watering of the stock, and he said no, he had no objection whatever. I should like to ask the minister two questions: Is there in existence to-day in Canada any law against Stock watering? When we say "stock watering," we mean that a company capitalized in the charter, say, at $2,000,000, issues and secures the subscription of just $1,000,000 in cash. That $1,000,000 is all it has and for many years it operates on that. It happens to strike successful days and the value of the stock on the gambling market advances. The proprietors of the concern then see an opportunity of skinning the public; so without adding another dollar of actual capital, they issue to themselves the balance of the authorized stock and in effect they create an artificial capital of $1,000,000 in addition to the actual capital of $1,000,000. Is there any law to prevent that, and if not, does the minister not think it is high time he provided such a law?

All I can say is that if that sort of transaction is carried out in any particular case and my hon. friend will bring the facts to the notice of the law officers of the crown, he will soon ascertain that there are such laws in this country; that that is fraud; that stock cannot be issued for nothing, and that those who do so are liable to be sent to the penitentiary. But I am not enforcing the criminal law of Canada. I am merely a humble secretary of state, the humble bobtail of the administration, attending as patiently as I can to the duties assigned to my department.

Owing to the applause I did not quite catch the minister's reply. May I ask him to repeat his

Supply-Secretary oj State
answer to my question: Is there a law that will prevent the actual transaction that I have described?
I do not think there is any doubt of that.
Will the minister tell us where it is?

My hon. friend should not ask me to name a particular section. Of course there is a law; the criminal law of this country applies. It is fraud to do that sort of thing and those who are indicted and found guilty of such fraud are sent to the penitentiary by the courts. I should like to refer hon. members to a recent case in England where, under a law similar to ours, Lord Kylsant, a prominent business man there, was sent to the penitentiary for improperly administering the affairs of his company.

It is amazing that we cannot bring about a similar situation in Canada; the minister seems unable to do so, so closely do we copy conditions in the United States, with all the evils that follow such exploitation there. May I suggest to him that if such a law exists, it is high time that he enforce it. I remember only a few years ago in this very house a lengthy debate on the British Empire Steel Corporation, when members of both political parties agreed, and so stated, that the British Empire Steel Corporation, at that time and previously, had been watered to the extent of $50,000,000, if my memory serves me correctly. It happened that it was the Minister of Labour in the Liberal government of the day who made this statement in the house. Surely some action could have been taken at that time, and hon. members ought not to be asked or expected by the minister to produce before him isolated cases. They are all around him; it is public knowledge that this sort of thing is being done. Debate aifter debate has taken place in the house on it. Hardly a year has passed without illustrations being given from this corner and supported by members in other parts of the house. I think the minister is hardly seized of the importance of doing away with this evil.

One of the greatest evils in
commercial life in this country is the watering of stocks and their sale to the public by financial pirates. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the case of the Canada Power and Paper Company. Has the Secretary of State power to investigate the operations of the men who formed that company and to inform the committee just what
was done, how it was done and who got awav with all the profits that should have gone to those who bought the bonds, and who. as the saying goes, were left holding the bag? Last year I put on the order paper a question asking for the amount of securities of the Canada Power and Paper Company and its subsidiaries held by life insurance companies. It was found that $10,000,000 of premiums paid by the people of Canada were invested in securities of this company and its subsidiaries. I believe a number of good paper companies in this country were ruined by the men who formed that organization. I do not knew whether it had a dominion charter or not. Would the Secretary of State inform us whether it had, whether anything was done in regard to the matter, and if not, whether anything can be done in the future? That is the important question.

I do not know of any way
by which you can prevent dishonest men from committing fraud so long as they may do it and still keep out of the penitentiary. It is not my duty to administer the criminal law. I told hon. gentlemen earlier in the debate that if a proper representation is made to me with respect to frauds committed by any company which has obtained a charter under the Companies Act of Canada, provision is made there for investigation, and since I have been in this office, for the first time in the history of Canada, such investigations have been carried out. They have cost large amounts of money, but they have shown that very grave frauds have been perpetrated, and now in the courts those who perpetrated or are alleged to have perpetrated those frauds are being brought to justice. If the hon. member has any case in mind and will bring it to the attention of the Secretary of State, I shall look into the matter carefully and advise him as best I can as to how those guilty of frauds may be brought to justice. But, as I say, I am not administering the criminal law of the country. I have no supervision over the people's morals, nor does it fall to my department to deal with such crimes as are committed. My time is occupied nearly sixteen hours out of every twenty-four in the performance of such duties as are committed to my care.
What we want in this country is a law to prevent these men watering these stocks. It has been done openly by, I think, hundreds of companies in Canada in the past.

I do not wish to be discourteous to my hon. friend, but when he
Supply-Secretary of State

talks as he is now doing about watering stocks I begin to wonder as to his knowledge of the matter. It is not the watering of stock that is the chief evil in this country. That is a minor evil, and sometimes when people complain about it without any knowledge of the facts I think they ought to be investigated to find out if they are afflicted with water on the brain.
I would ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw that statement.

I do not know
whether I am one of those whose brains ought to be investigated;, it is quite possible a good many of us may be in that position, but we happen to represent here a considerable number whose brains are of pretty much the same calibre as ours, and we confess quite frankly that we are at an utter loss to know just what to do when we come to a matter of this kind. The Secretary of State rather suggests to us that this whole matter should be left to the courts to decide, but the point we are trying to make is that there is no legislation at the present time adequate to deal with a situation that actually exists. Everyone in this house knows perfectly well that it is next to impossible for a private member to introduce legislation on a matter of this importance with any hope that it will be passed. We cannot even be sure that it will get to a committee; some of us indeed are doubtful whether a bill we sponsor will even get a chance for first reading. Under these circumstances it seems as if we must lay upon the government the responsibility of introducing legislation along this line, and I feel that the Secretary of State, who has to deal with companies, is the one to whom we ought to look for action. Further than that, it is all very well for the Secretary of State to imply that the same kind of action is possible in the big cases as in the small cases, but I respectfully submit that in practice that is not so. It is not possible for a small shareholder to engage a lawyer who will stand any chance whatever against the legal talent that may be engaged by a great corporation. The poor man who has only a few dollars behind him cannot possibly go into a fight against a great corporation, and I do not think it is clarifying the situation for the Secretary of States to suggest that his idea and mine of law are abysmally apart. I do not think that that helps us very much. I want to bring a matter to his attention for the sake of illustration. I happened to find among my papers an editorial from the Manitoba Free Press referring to a particular matter which illustrates the fog in which the

public now finds itself; and if some of us here need our brains examined, I presume the editor of the Free Press also needs his investigated. This editorial-I have not the date-says:	.
When the searchlight is finally turned upon the many deals and transactions that lie in the wake of the moribund Canada Power and Paper corporation, it must be hoped that special attention will be given to the details of the spectacular Anticosti purchase which created a flurry of public attention in the summer of 1926. Nine millions of dollars of the public's money were paid for the securities of the Anticosti corporation which appeared to be backed by the strongest kind of pledges of three important paper companies. That money has in part disappeared, and the Securities Protective Committee contents itself in its circular letter by saying: "As a result of this acquisition by the new company of the undertakings and assets of all companies concerned . . . the Anticosti stumpage agreement will be automatically extinguished."
This is not good enough. Holders of the old 61 per cent Anticosti bonds are to be given new 5J per cent bonds. They therefore, lose substantial amounts of their capital. Holders of the 7 per cent Anticosti preference shares are to get one and a half shares of new common stock for each share previously held. They lose much of their capital, and must accept also junior securities. They are entitled now to the full truth of the Anticosti deal. They must be at least permitted to learn why they have lost their money. Surely this is not asking too much.
The editorial then goes in some detail into the history of the company and its operations, and concludes:
It is now time to throw light upon it. The public is entitled to know, for instance, how much was actually paid for Senator Menier's game preserve. It is entitled to know how much water was poured into the securities issued rvith the island as security. It is entitled to know the costs of cutting pulpwood there. It is entitled to learn whether or not the men who swung the deal exercised sound business judgment. It must know if they are safe persons with whom to invest money in the future.
The time has come for a thorough housecleaning in our financial methods, and the Canada Power and Paper collapse is an excellent reason for beginning it.
That is just one illustration of what is taking place right along. What the public wants to know is what is to be done about it, and we ask the Secretary of State, who grants the charters, whether there is any way by which the public may have some idea whether or not the stock of a company so chartered offers a safe investment. I do not think that we are unreasonable in urging him to consider bringing down legislation that will do something in this regard.

I do not wish to prolong the discussion, but there is legislation at the

Supply-Secretary oj State
present time which provides a certain procedure for investigation. For instance, during the past year I instituted an investigation which was very extensive indeed with respect to one of the largest operating corporations in Canada, the Yukon Consolidated Gold Corporation, with a paid-up capital of S6,000,000. I would make exactly the same kind of examination if it were a capital of 86,000 if application were made to me. The public know very well where the facts can be ascertained. If the Canada Power and Paper Company has been incorporated under the Companies Act, then the documents will be on file with reference to the acquisition of the properties for which stock was issued. The facts can be easily ascertained. The later events are found in the court, because if my memory is correct the court approved of the compromise arrangement to which the editor of the Free Press objected in the editorial which my hon. friend has just read. The whole matter was before the court and is a matter of court record; there the real facts can be obtained. But I know of no way in which the Secretary of State can supervise the purchase of, say, Anticosti island, or can properly appreciate the price which should be paid for it. I have no interest in the matter, but men who are competent to judge at the time the land was purchased told me that it had been purchased much below its value, that it was a most valuable acquisition, and that the revenue from its timber and other resources would bring in ample revenue. They told me that they had had its timber resources inspected by very competent experts and that they had the utmost confidence in the undertaking. I know friends of mine invested many thousands of dollars, believing that the reports of those experts would ultimately be realized. Apart from fraud, I know of no way of protecting men against making purchases of timber or mining or other natural resources which in the future may not realize the exaggerated hopes entertained at the time of the purchase. But if any person will allege fraud in regard to the Canada Power and Paper Company, and apply to the Secretary of State in the formal manner provided, I can, if it is incorporated under the Companies Act and unless the company is now out of existence, order a most complete inquiry and investigation with respect to every fact. Time and time again I have so advised men who have made complaints to me. I cannot investigate and imperil the financial stability and credit of companies which are being honestly administered, simply because some newspaper makes reflections upon them; but if fraud is alleged,
then there is a way under the procedure laid down in the Companies Act to conduct such investigation. In every case where applications have been made to me an investigation has been conducted.

A few years ago several
of the provinces sought federal legislation with the aim of meeting this difficulty of watered stock-otherwise called "blue sky" legislation. Their position was that without concurrent legislation by the; parliament of Canada they had no control over companies operating under federal charters. What help or encouragement did the provinces get from the Secretary of State in regard to the legislation they proposed?

They got just as little
encouragement for the proposition they made to me as they obtained from my predecessor. They asked me to introduce a bill which would transfer certain matters out of the federal jurisdiction into the jurisdiction of the provinces. I told them the proposal was ridiculous, and that no bill that I might introduce could transfer legislative jurisdiction from this parliament to the provincial legislatures. But I also told them that, as soon as they might reasonably desire, the Dominion government, through the Prime Minister, was prepared to call a conference of the representatives of the provincial governments in order to discuss constitutional amendments by which the jurisdiction might be vested in the parliament of Canada in respect to certain matters and in the provincial legislatures in respect to other matters. That was the only answer I could possibly give them.

I am glad the Secretary
of State has told the committee that the Prime Minister intends to take this matter up with the provinces at some future date. Has the minister had many complaints during the last two years with regard to watered stock?

We made the most complete investigation, covering fifteen months, in the case of one company, in the course of which we brought witnesses from England and from the ends of Canada to give evidence before a commissioner appointed for the purpose. We are carrying on these investigations from time to time in the department. We do not publish the results in the newspapers, although they are given to the newspapers, and sometimes short memoranda appear with respect to them.

Has the minister investigated the collapse of the Swedish match
Supply-Secretary of State

trust and its relation .to any stock transactions affecting any Canadian company? If not, is it the intention of his department to do so?

The hon. gentleman should
advertise his question in the amusement columns of the newspapers.
Oh, oh.
I have no knowledge of any Swedish match trust being incorporated under the Companies Act of Canada.

I think my question is
perfectly proper. I have read in the newspapers that investigations of the Swedish match trust are being conducted all over the world, and I am sure there must be some Canadian transactions connected with that trust. I am putting my question in all seriousness. I think when a fair question is asked the minister should give a decent answer, even though he is getting like the Prime Minister-vexed at everything.
I am never vexed.

When I ask a question
I do not want to be insulted by the Secretary of State.

If the hon. member thinks
I insulted him I most humbly apologize. I was not vexed when I made the remark to which my hon. friend takes objection, for I am never angry; but I am not aware that the Swedish match trust is organized under any Canadian charter.
I accept the Secretary of State's apology, Mr. Chairman.

It is gratifying, Mr. Chcdr-man, to know that this session private legislation with regard to companies is very limited. When some companies come to parliament with a private bill there is often a nigger in the woodpile, and that is why private bills must always be very thoroughly scrutinized. This applies not only to private bills presented to this parliament, but also to similar bills presented to the provincial legislatures. As I say, it is a good thing this session that we have very little private legislation on the order paper. As federal and provincial company law differs in many respects, it is a great mistake to have companies chartered both provincially and federally. The promoters of such companies should make their choice at the time they organize, in order that the public may know whether the companies are provincial or federal in character. This is of the utmost importance, and I cannot understand
[Mr. Beaubien.J
why a company should be acting under the provisions of both federal and provincial statutes. I do not say this with regard to the present minister; I say it objectively and not subjectively, but when there is some trouble in cases where companies have obtained powers both federal and provincial, at times we are told by the officials of the company that it is a provincial concern, but when we communicate with the provincial secretary we are told that it is a federal concern. No one knows where he is with such hybrid organizations. This is why I respectfully suggest that the Secretary of State be very careful about granting charters to companies which already have been organized under provincial laws. In some cases there are regulations with regard to reports and other matters, such as the number of directors, the capital subscribed and so on, which it is impossible to get but which are essential when we have to deal with these companies.

I feel that some of the suggestions which have been made to-night have gone over the minister's head. Possibly they have entered his mind, but I do not think so. I believe the minister as a rule, when he understands a question, is very gentlemanly and courteous and ready to answer, so I think he must have misunderstood some of the matters which have been brought up. I just want to direct his attention to the fact that, in connection with the Canada Power and Paper Company the Financial Post of September 26 last stated that the security holders' protective committee had a plan for the reorganization of the corporation which would cut its capitalization from $103,000,000 to $52,000,000. The article concluded by saying that with the final winding up of the company there would pass out of existence an enterprise which was not a credit to the Canadian corporation field.
The suggestion which I was trying to make to the minister was that if proper supervision was exercised over the capitalization of these companies before they started operations it would save a lot of grief to the investing public in Canada, and would help maintain the confidence of Canadian investors in Canadian corporations. It is very unfortunate that investors in Canada should be compelled to run the risks they do run at present because of what seems to be a very decided difference of opinion between the federal Secretary of State and the different provincial governments, each wanting to .have control of the issuing of charters. I would simply say to the minister that the dominion should refuse incorporation to companies who ask for too large a capitalization for the assets which they possess.

Supply-Secretary oj State
If provincial governments want to give charters to companies which are improperly financed and capitalized, leit the provincial governments take 'the responsibility for so doing. As far as the dominion is concerned, it is time we exercised some supervision, and if necessary introduced legislation which would give the Secretary of State power to supervise the issuing of capital or even debenture stock or bonds by these corporations. I do not think the legislation on the statute books to-day gives the minister the right to exercise that supervision which I think should be exercised, and I suggest that if he has not that authority under the present law he might very well introduce such legislation in this house. It is not open to any private member to do so, since it would involve the expenditure of money, so we can only urge this suggestion upon the minister.

I can only tell my hon.
friend-
Shall the item carry?
Carried.

A few moments ago the
Secretary of State told the committee that one investigation with regard to watered stock was being made. He also said that if complaint was made by anyone with regard to watered stock, an investigation would be made.
