I did not want the names of the companies, but I wanted to know if a dozen or a score or more complaints had been made, *because from the way the public have been dealt with in the last two or three years it seems .to me they do not know they have the right and privilege to have inquiry made by the Secretary of State. I should be glad if the minister would tell the committee whether he has had any considerable number of complaints which would show that the public know of the privileges and rights which are theirs.

I can simply repeat what I said before, that since I came into office in August, 1930, we have made a very careful supervision of the terms of the charters issued. During that time only two complaints have been made to my office of the nature suggested by the hon. gentleman.
I hope that after to-night the Secretary of State will be pestered by complaints of those who have suffered from the effect of watered stock in investments.

Item agreed to.
Patent record, $25,000.

Do the fees received from those who apply for patents meet the expenses of running the office?
Supply-Secretary oj State

I cannot at the moment distinguish between patents and copyrights, but the revenue is half a million a year and it goes into the consolidated revenue account. Therefore we have to ask for an appropriation from parliament for the expenses.
Who is in charge of the patent office?
Mr. Richard, he has been there many years.

Item agreed to.
International office for the protection of industrial property, international copyright union office and union for the protection of literary and artistic works, $2,000.
How is that money distributed? Is it paid in a lump sum or is it distributed to various institutions?
It is a contribution made by this country under the Berne convention. It has been outstanding for many years.

Item agreed to.
Expenses under the Canada Temperance Act,
Explain.

There are only three constituencies in Canada in which the Canada Temperance Act applies, but in case application is made for a repeal in any of these constituencies there has to be an election. Every year it is customary to put in the estimates an amount to pay the expenses of [DOT] such an election, although one is very seldom held.
Can the minister name the constituencies?

I know there is one in Quebec, Thetford Mines, and there are two others.
I shall have to ask the hon. gentleman to wait until to-morrow for the answer.

I must confess to ignorance of the application of the Canada Temperance Act. In what way does it apply in certain isolated instances? Do those particular constituencies come under a federal act instead of under provincial legislation?

There was passed at one time an act known as the Canada Temperance Act, by which counties or constituencies, were authorized to adopt that act. It was adopted by many constituencies throughout Canada. Under the same act they could vote themselves out of its jurisdiction, and as the years went by the constituencies voted themselves out except in three specific instances. These are still under the act.

I assume that this is what they used to call the old Scott Act. Are these particular constituencies, which must be within some province or other, exempt from the operation of the ordinary provincial legislation?
I shall have to refer that question to the Minister of Justice.
Item agreed to.
Salaries, $260,766; contingencies, $30,000.

I should like to have a statement from the minister with regard to the reported influx into this country of a considerable number of boys, I think it is some five hundred. How many are being admitted, and w'hy should they be admitted under the conditions which now exist in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Acting Minister of Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The newspaper reports with respect to the admission of boys-I must make it plain that they are British boys- cast no reflection at all upon the policy of the Department of Immigration. I think I can probably satisfy the hon. member by saying that as severe a restriction has been placed upon migrants coming to Canada as has ever been enforced by the department. For many years associations have been established for the purpose of bringing people to Canada from other lands. These associations have grown up and have spent large amounts of money and there is no doubt that from time to time they have brought people to this country who have proven to foe very acceptable. These associations have not confined their activities to any one race, but mainly have had to do with British peoples.
In connection with the matter referred to by the hon. member, I will say that the provinces have been consulted with respect to what migrants they could absorb, what prospects would be offered to migrants for getting on in the world, or the possibility of their contributing something to the settlement of our vacant lands. The British boys referred to by the newspaper articles are being brought out at the request of the province of Ontario. I interviewed the various agencies and pointed out that we were passing through a time when these boys might meet with obstacles which would give them a good deal of trouble, that perhaps they would not have the same chance as the immigrant who came to Canada a few years ago, and under these circumstances immigration into Canada should be restricted until such time as the outlook might be more

Supply-Immigration
attractive. These various associations embrace the United Church of Canada, the Roman Catholic church and other bodies, and their activities have been known to the department. They first asked for 800 boys, but I stipulated that the maximum movement should be 500, and it will not reach anything like that number. I was satisfied with their assurances that these boys would take up vocations provided for them by the different asso-v iations and would not be a charge upon the country. I am not persuaded at all that Canada is at a point where she can refuse admission to any desirable people, particularly British people.

It is hardly necessary to point out that there are thousands of our Dwn boys just leaving public and high school who find it impossible to dbtain work. They are qualified for farm, office or factory work, but they cannot find openings. It seems to me a very doubtful policy indeed to permit boys from any other country, Great Britain included, to come to this country to take work away from our own Canadian boys, who will then have to walk the streets.
What ages are these boys?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Mostly between the ages of sixteen and eighteen.

Mr. Chairman, I want to protest in as vigorous a manner as ever I have done in this house against the bringing in of these boys. I have not the words at my command to express my utter disapproval of the policy of bringing teen age boys and girls to this country, particularly boys. Only the other day I happened to have the opportunity of studying a report of the Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare and I find that in the city of Toronto when the single unemployed were registered during the first great registration, some 12-5 per cent of the total single unemployed were boys of teen age, between sixteen and twenty years, the majority of whom were immigrants who had been brought to this country within the previous few years. That condition in the city of Toronto must reflect the general state of affairs throughout the country and should justify the complete abolition of this policy. The minister will find in every principal city in Canada orphan homes out of which numbers of boys and girls who have reached the age when they are required to leave the institution are being dismissed yearly. These boys and girls cannot be taken care of, yet we proceed to pour in hundreds of other boys from the old country. I w'onder if the minister realizes
that there is hardly a province which does not require more and better facilities for the taking care of our own boys and girls?
I think the policy of bringing these young people into this country to work for farmers is nothing short of brutal. Case after case can be cited where extreme hardship has resulted, and the mere excuse, as will doubtless be provided by the minister, that there is inspection, is not sufficient. When an inspector visits a farm he cannot expect a boy who has to live with the farmer to tell the truth if there is any danger of the farmer finding it out. The result is that these boys run away, get into the cities, and add to the .present unemployment problem. I have protested against this matter at every opportunity, and I repeat my protests to-night and ask the minister to reconsider his stand on the matter.

Mr. Chairman, I have
no desire to prolong this debate, but since the government now in power, through the mouths of its representatives during the last elections, protested so strongly against the policy adopted by the former administration, I feel it my duty to protest against the policy adopted by the minister. It has been said throughout the country, and particularly in the province of Quebec, that the government which preceded the one now in office was responsible for the hard times and unemployment which existed, because of the fact that too many immigrants had been permitted to enter the country. I think it is my duty as a representative of the people of my constituency, and more especially voicing the sentiments of Quebec, to protest most strongly against the government allowing and helping these boys, even British boys, to come to Canada under present circumstances. There is nso doubt, from the figures that have been given by hon. members who have preceded me, and having regard to the conditions that obtain in the west and also in Ontario, that these young boys who have been allowed to enter Canada will not be a source of help, but in the course of a few weeks or the next few months, or perhaps in a few years, will, as has happened to others in the past, not find enough work to support themselves and probably will become public charges, of which under present circumstances we have already too many. We are told there is no place where our boys who leave college or their own homes, can earn their living; there is no chance for a boy from Quebec who goes to Ontario to meet his people, if he has any there, to find employment and earn his living; and yet we are allowing boys from the other

Supply-Immigration

side to come in. Even if they are good boys, nevertheless they become surplus labour in Quebec, Ontario and other parts of Canada to which they may drift in the future. I strongly protest against the policy of the present administration, which is lacking in its duty and not fulfilling the promises made during the last election, when hon. members opposite said that if they were returned to power they would see that the flow of immigration which was the cause of the present depression would be stopped.

I should like to ask the minister as to the policy of the department with regard to a phase of the immigration question which has not been mentioned here to-night and which, as a matter of fact, is directly opposed to what might be called immigration. I refer to the subject of deportation. I am quite in accord with any policy that restricts, to the extreme, immigration to Canada at this time, having regard to the depression and the prevailing unemployment. But many deportations are made by the department, I understand at the request of the representatives of the municipalities. I offer no objection to the deportation of foreigners who are undesirable, but I should like to say a word on behalf of a certain class of people who came to this country in good faith, at a time when we wanted them to come, and who have been here perhaps only two, three or four years, not sufficiently long to qualify them for naturalization and citizenship. Some of them, through no fault of their own, though quite willing to work if employment can be obtained, have been placed in the unfortunate position of being deported. There are those who consider, I believe quite honestly, that a man who is not a citizen and who has become a public charge should be returned to the country of his birth. I am not quite in sympathy with that view. When men have come to Canada in good faith, perhaps at the invitation of the federal government; have taken employment, have conducted themselves properly, and would no doubt in due time, just as soon as possible, become Canadian citizens; and when, through no fault of their own but because of the depression that now reigns in this country, they lose their employment as many native-born citizens have done, we should apply the greatest judgment, generosity, fairness and justice to any proposal that they be deported. What is the minister's policy when a request comes, let us say from a municipality, that a certain list of residents, foreigners, who have been here a short time, be deported on the ground that they have become public charges? Does the

department deport them without further investigation? Or does it make inquiries of its own, and if so, upon what principle does it act before deporting those people?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
When I assumed administration of the Immigration department, the situation as I found it in regard to the working out of the question was one which I have never agreed with since I have been able to comprehend the meaning of migration to this country. The question that has just been raised by the hon. member has, of course, given me a good deal of concern. Every case is dealt with upon its merits. In the past, through various influences, through different policies that were adopted, it was thought that the solution of our country's troubles was to encourage people from any quarter of the globe to come to Canada, and for this purpose assisted passages were given and concessions were granted here and there. That policy was not new; it was followed by the United States for many years, and some ten or fifteen years ago they saw the fallacy of it. This government, however, adopted an attitude which I think should be commended. When we came into power, having regard to the fact that we had through various agencies allowed people to come into this country, sometimes as a result of representations made by people not under the direct control of the government of the day, we found ourselves confronted with a situation that was not very comfortable to say the least. Rightly or wrongly, I came to the conclusion that we should take drastic steps to control immigration, from the standpoint, not of pure materialism, but of trying to control our population so that in the future we may be able to say that we have attracted to Canada those best calculated to build up a strong and virile country. So far as I am concerned, that policy has been very sturdily pursued. I am not unmindful of the difficulties involved in the point raised by the hon. member, because I have to deal with such matters every day. Men have been attracted to Canada; they have come here expecting to find work and oportunities far beyond those available to them in their own country. At times they have undoubtedly been induced to come here by promises made by those who in the past had agreements with various transportation companies, promises that could not be fulfilled. That is a burden which the government of Canada, must assume. We have at present in this country from many lands, hundreds of thousands, many of them splendid people, but many of them, I must reluctantly admit, such as we could well do without. We have many people representative of many races; we are faced with the problem of divided families,

Supply-Immigration
with part of the family in Europe or elsewhere and part of it here, with all the hardship that that involves. Even though we are confronted with a severe depression it will take a great deal of argument to convince me that we have to shut the door to migrants from the British Isles who want to come here, paying their own way, taking care of themselves and bringing money with them, although that is an indifferent matter compared with the spirit that prompts them to come. So far as I am concerned, while at the present time we encourage no one to come here until we clean up at home the mess that was left with us, I want to say to the committee that there will be no shutting of the door to British immigration.

I am not sure that the hon. gentleman answered my question. I should like to know the policy of the department in respect to deportations. Does the department accept the recommendations made by municipalities as to deportations, or does it make further inquiry as to the merits of each individual case?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: When a complaint comes in to the department-and under the Immigration Act these complaints come from the clerks of municipalities-against people who have contravened the provisions of the Immigration Act, it is investigated by the officers of the department, and until the case has been finally decided and an appeal has been allowed or dismissed, no deportation takes place. There never has been a deportation of people from this country without careful investigation beforehand.

I do not wish to be misunderstood. I have no complaint whatsoever to make with regard to deportations of a delinquent or a man who has committed a crime and is consequently deported after he has served his sentence. I am referring entirely to those who, merely by reason of the fact that they cannot find employment, but would otherwise make desirable citizens, are reported to the department, and I am asking whether in such cases they are deported.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I know of no case where
deportation has taken place of a desirable citizen simply because he has become a public charge through inability to find employment.
I do not know of any such case.

It is very refreshing indeed to hear the opposition criticizing the immigration policy of this government. I presume that if it had not been for the 750,000 im-
41761-142J
migrants who were brought into this country by the late government during the last six, seven, or eight years, we would not have had such an unemployment problem on our hands to-day. However, my immediate point is this: There seems to be a direct attack tonight against permitting five hundred British boys to enter Canada. Surely bon. gentlemen opposite are straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel. On behalf of those boys in my constituency I just wish to say that we have boys of sixteen to eighteen years of age who came through the Vimy Ridge farm at Guelph and latterly from Norval near Brampton, and in the last four years I have been responsible for bringing some fifty-five of these boys to my constituency. I wish to bear testimony to-night, Mr. Chairman, that my county is very proud of those boys. They came from selected families in the old country and came because they had a desire to learn farming out here, not to tell the boss how to farm or how they do it "over We," but to learn farming as it is done in this country. There may have been one or two or three of them who have gone to the city, but if they have I do not know it, and I keep in close touch with these boys. The farmers in my county want more of them. I had one boy who came to a farmer in my county and stayed two years, grew robust, learned farming and then returned home to England, and he is now one of the greatest boosters Canada has. Another young man succeeded him, and this fall after two years with the same farmer he goes to the agricultural college at Guelph to pursue his further studies there.
I cannot understand why hon. gentlemen who are always talking about doing something that might block any arrangement we might make with the empire at the coming imperial conference, should just a few weeks before that conference meets tell the world that we cannot take five hundred clean British boys and assimilate them here. I think we can do it in the province of Ontario if they are not wanted elsewhere. I could not let this opportunity pass, Mr. Chairman, without stating the .position of the farmers in my county. When hon. gentlemen opposite speak of the unemployed in the cities, there is not a farmer who can go into the cities and find very many boys who want to go out to the country and, learn farming. Most of the farmers in my constituency who apply for boys who do not smoke; they do not want cigarettes being smoked around their buildings. In the ranks of the unemployed in the cities I do not think you could find a young fellow who knows which end of the horse to put a
Supply-Immigration,

collar on, and itbey do not want to know; they do not want to learn farming. So it is ridiculous for hon. gentlemen apposite to say that these British boys are taking employment from those who are to be found in the ranks of the unemployed in our cities. I just rose, Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the few hundred boys who have come to my constituency in the last ten years, to say that they are a very fine type of citizen, and that the farmers in my county are asking for more of them.

I have been amazed to hear my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration for the second time during the present session refer to his arduous endeavours to clean up the mess that was left on bis doorstep when the late government went out of office. The only impression that his remarks have left upon me is that they are redolent of his self-appointed pasture. I wish to ask my hon. friend from North Huron who was a member of the opposition in 1929, what was his attitude on that occasion with regard to the stand taken by the leader of his own party in regard to immigration into Canada. The present Minister of Immigration was not a member of the house at that time, but my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce was here, and for the information of the committee may I just quote the words of his own right hon. leader in a debate in this house just a few short months before his party faced the Canadian people in the election of 1930. It is well known in the minister's own department that the policy of effective restriction of which he now prates so highly, had already been put into effect by the late administration before he was honoured by the portfolio of minister. Here is what the Prime Minister of Canada, then leader of the opposition, said in this house of February 11, 1929, at page 22 of Hansard, speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne:
We have here one of the largest undeveloped areas in the world; we have a very pressing necessity for more people. There need be no misapprehension about that, notwithstanding what has been said from time to time to the contrary.
Then listen to this:
It will be found that the increase of population in this country brought about through bringing additional people in will not only lessen unemployment for those who are now in it, but will increase all employment.
Where are my Tory friends now? Where is the member for North Huron who would not swallow a camel?

In answer to the hon.
member for Vancouver Centre
Mr. Chairman-
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member asked me a question.
The hon. member for North Huron may reply when I am through.

The hon. member asked
me a question twice, Mr. Chairman, and I should like to-

My hon.
friend can answer all the questions he likes when I sit down. My hon. friend from North Huron said that we were straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel. By his silence during the speech of his own leader, now the Prime Minister of Canada, he not only swallowed a camel-he swallowed a whole camel corps. During the session of 1929 the then leader of the opposition, now Prime Minister, a few short months before the general election of 1930, used these words, as recorded in Hansard, that the bringing into Canada of immigrants would not only lessen unemployment but would increase employment all through the dominion. Let me quote him further at page 23:
Mr. Bennett:	The minister says: "Hear,
hear." The responsibility rests with him and his government. We have no power to control the expenditures; we have no power over the money of this country; but all I can say is that "when in the fullness of time that power is entrusted to those who sit to the left of the Speaker, they wall deal with the immigration problem in a different manner.
And what was that different manner? The general organizer of the Tory party, who is now a distinguished member of the Senate, introduced into this house a resolution for bringing in 300,000 immigrants to settle the vast spaces of our western prairies. The government spent millions of dollars last year in Saskatchewan to help the destitute. How many millions of dollars would it have cost this Tory government if the plans of its general organizer had been put into effect?
Now, sir, my versatile and volatile friend the Minister of Railways gave expression to this perfect gem, and I hope my friend from North Huron will remember it. I am quoting from page 2746 of Hansard of May 22, 1929:
My complaint is not so much that the number of British immigrants is not larger, as that our immigration of all classes is much too small. The question is often asked: how; many can we absorb in this country? I submit that w-e can absorb as many as we can put at useful occupations and as many as vre can handle without crowding out the other classes of the people already here, whether they be farmers or labouring people. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that

Supply-I mmigration
we could take many times the numbers of people of all kinds than we are getting at the present time.
That was the official policy of the Conservative party a few months before they went to the country in 1930.
Quote it again.

I am
going to quote another passage which is equally significant. At page 2752 of Hansard in the same speech the present Minister of Railways said:
It is obvious to my mind that the government has not a satisfactory immigration policy. If Canada is to grow, prosper, and progress, it is the duty of this government to awaken to its responsibilities and really try to bring down an immigration policy adequate to the needs of this dominion.
That, Mr. Chairman, was the policy of the present Prime Minister in 1929, that was the policy of the Minister of Railways in 1929, that was the policy of the distinguished organizer of the Conservative party in 1929, that was the policy of every single member of the Conservative party who supported his leader in this house in 1929. Then in 1930 they went to the country on a diametrically opposite policy, and yet the Minister of Immigration has the audacity to come to this committee this evening-
Oh, oh.

He has
the audacity to come to this committee this evening and talk about the "mess" left upon his doorstep. If there were too many immigrants brought into Canada in the three or four years preceding 1930, the fault lies not with the then administration but with the official opposition of that day; for if their recommendations had been hearkened to we would have had ten, twenty, yes, one hundred times as many immigrants as were admitted -and then the Minister of Immigration would have had on his doorstep that "mess" to which he has referred twice this session. I hope the members of the Conservative party will read the record of what passed in this chamber in the session of 1929, for then they will realize that the work of the late administration was effective in restricting the flow of immigration, although in taking that course they had to fight against the pressure put upon them by the leaders of the Conservative party to flood Canada with immigrants for a period of five, six or seven years.

Mr. Chairman, early in the discussion the Minister of Immigration said that no one was deported until he had had an opportunity to appeal to the department. The case which I am about to deal with has to do with the city from which I come, and I think there are many like it. The lady in this instance had been in Canada for over twenty years, she was married in this country and had three children, whose present ages are eighteen, seventeen and fifteen; she developed fits and was put into an institution at Woodstock Ontario; she was deported on October 3, 1931, and was on the way to Great Britain before her husband even knew what had happened. What is the policy of this department with respect to the husband and three children who are left in the dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I cannot identify 'the case to which the hon. member refers, but for his information I may say that the deportation of people to their country of origin is not done in any autocratic, cruel way, such as might be inferred from his remarks. They are given every opportunity, so far as I know, because their cases come under review time and again, with a view to finding out what responsibility this country has to take care of these poor unfortunates who find themselves in mental difficulty and have to be put in mental hospitals. I am sure the hon. member recognizes that the province of Ontario and the other provinces have spent many millions of dollars in order to treat and take care of mental cases. I think it is incumbent on the other nations of the world to take a leaf out of the provinces' book and to assume their responsibilities in this regard. I can assure the hon. member that no case that I have any recollection of has not received very careful consideration by the department in an effort to place the responsibility where it lies. As these cases come up every day it is impossible for me to identify this particular case.

These cases are well
known in the section of the country from which I come. What the people of Hamilton most object to with respect to this case-it was widely discussed last year-was the separation of the mother from her husband and her children without their knowledge. We want to know what is to become of the three children. It was at least the bounden duty of the department to let the husband know that his wife was going to be deported. I would like to say that the lady in question is living the life of a normal human being in England, and is not in any institution of any kind at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
give me the name?
Sup-ply-Immigration
I will give the minister the name.

I should like to ask the minister what is the policy with regard to divided families. He mentioned the problem . of bringing divided families together, and I should like to ask if a man in this country who has a close relative in a European country other than Great Britain has a chance of getting that relative out to Canada at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The policy of the department with respect to the union of divided families is first to investigate closely that part of the family residing in Canada. If on hvestigation we find that the person in Can-

ada is acceptable in ithe view of the departmental officials and of myself, and that the person sought to be brought to Canada will not disturb or be a burden upon labour in this country, then a recommendation is made to council and an appropriate order in council is passed. All those orders in council are available to hon. members of the house. Of course, of necessity that policy must be relaxed when we get through this depression.

I believe the minister did not quite understand the question of the hon. member for Medicine Hat. I think what the hon. member	meant was	this: If	a manand his wife in	this country	have a	boy or
girl in the old country, and that child has reached the age of twenty-one years, I believe they cannot bring the child to Canada because of some regulation enacted in the past. I should like to ask if a father or a mother can bring a boy or a girl of twenty-two years of age from Poland or Roumania to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Not as a matter of right. We are charged with trying to preserve, for the present at	least, the	labour	marketin Canada for	persons at	present	within
Canada. While it may occasion some distress to (parents to be unalble to bring their twenty-two year old boy to this country, yet we must preserve to the people who are here what labour is available to them. However, I hope that is not a policy which will have to be pursued for a very long time. Each case is dealt with on its merits, but the underlying principle is this: If the person sought to be brought to Canada is likely to take a position in the labour market here which will displace some person alreadjy legally and properly in Canada, then the reunion will have to be postponed until things take a different turn.

I just want to ask the minister a question in connection with the speech he made in this house on February 23. At page 440 of Hansard I find the following words:
. . . whether we like it or not, we must get over to the positive side of immigration, because we must have more people if we hope to pay off the debt with which ten million people are loaded at present by reason of the railroad problem on our hands.
Is that the policy of the government?
Mr. Chairman-

I would like an answer to my question, because this matter has been the subject of discussion in the labour movement in the city in which I reside. What

Supply-Immigration
is the policy of the Minister of Immigration in connection with the announcement he made in this house this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I do not know that I need add much to what I said on that occasion. Anyone who has followed the debates in this house and who has an appreciation of the different railway and road services that have been created in this country, preceding settlement, must recognize that in order to get the fullest advantage of them, and indeed to pay for them, people must be colonized along those services. I do not think the hon. member need have any great fear that in its administration of the immigration laws the present government will induce to come to Canada people who are likely to disturb the labour market. But we have an immense country. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre blamed the situation upon someone on this side of the house, and charged me with blaming it on members on the other side of the house. That really does not mean much to m-e, because at present I am administering this department, and my task is to colonize the people at home, with full knowledge of the fact that without an increased population, carefully selected-which may be a slow process-this may be difficult.
That is what I meant by the positive side of immigration. We will ultimately get to the point where we will have a population which properly colonized, will be able to share the burden of debt which has arisen from the public services we have projected and made available to the people of this country. That is the policy of the government.

I gather from the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre that the policy of the Conservative party in 1929 was wrong. If that is so, I presume the party will be commended for changing their policy and getting on the right track now. With respect to permitting teen age boys to come to Canada, I appreciate the difficulties with which the government is faced when these youths are brought in from Great Britain. It is a serious matter. I also appreciate the difficulty in putting into force rules or regulations which perhaps would interfere with the good will and good feeling which exist between Canada and the old country at the present time. Possibly a gentle hint from the minister or from the government to the authorities responsible in the old countrj', or those who are thinking of bringing these jmuths to Canada, might have the desired effect without the necessity of there being any binding rules or regulations adopted by the Department of Immigration.
I notice quite a decrease in the amount asked for this year. Can the minister tell us where the cut has been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The decrease is due to the abolition of certain offices: one chief clerk; one woman officer; one clerk retired; two clerks, grade four; one clerk, grade three; four stenographers, grade two; two typists, grade two; one typist, grade one; one clerk, grade two; one messenger. Then, of course, there is the ten per cent reduction in salaries.

A year ago the minister made a statement with regard to the placement of families in various provinces under his back to the land policy, which he advocated. Has he any information to give the committee now?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Rightly or wrongly-I do not know whether hon. members will agree with me-it became apparent to me when I assumed my present office that there were and would continue to be in increasing numbers people unemployed who were formerly engaged in industry. In Canada we had many families who had farm experience and who had gone to the cities, attracted there by high wages. They found themselves out of employment and although they had some money it was dwindling through payment of rents and so on. I thought it desirable to enlist the services of the railway companies and of those who had theretofore been interested in immigration, with a view to coordinating the efforts of all. The purpose was, by helping people to select vacant farms, of which we had many thousands, to enable them to go back to the land and become selfsupporting. Someone may disagree with that and say that that is not the place in which to become self reliant. I am not prepared yet to agree with those who hold that view. However, we did meet with a measure of success, which I think is commendable. Many people who found themselves out of work, with some money and with farm experience and an agricultural background, joined in the effort and went back to the land. The latest figures we have, so far as the railways and the department are concerned, show that just under fifty thousand people are back on the land to-day. That comprises families who have taken up farms, and about fourteen thousand single men who are working on the farms of Canada.
Where did they go?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I could scarcely trace the fifty thousand.

Tell us where some went.
Supply-Immigration
What proportion established themselves in certain parts of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I will come to that. The department pursued the project which it outlined for itself in the fall of 1930 and, I believe, every province in Canada followed in the wake. Certainly Ontario and Quebec did, as well as the western provinces, and the maritime provinces, in a measure. I have not the figures as to what they have done, but if any hon. member would like to have the figures which the railways and the Immigration department have for the farm placements, they are available, because we have kept complete records of each family, where they have gone, what wages they are receiving, and so on. I do not think that the families would care to have their names heralded from the housetops. They are receiving no help from the government. They are doing all right and are going to make good.
Would the minister be good enough to table in the near future a report of that transaction so that we will know where we are?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to
table a report, but I do not want to give the names of the people who have gone to the farms.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That is their own business.
The minister could state how many had settled in each locality.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes, but not their names.

I think the minister knows what he wants to convey, but there seems to be a misunderstanding in the committee as to what he is actually conveying. When the minister speaks of settling these people on farms, does he mean settling single men as hired men, or is he referring to those placed on abandoned farms? If the latter, I should like to know where those abandoned farms are, because I do not know of a single instance where this has taken place. Is the minister referring to the single men placed under the provisions of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, where the farmers were paid by the government for the keep of the men?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
No, I have no reference
to that. The families which have been settled on farms consist of people who had sufficient money to go back to the land under the

guidance of the railways and the department. I was not referring to the single men placed on farms and assisted by government gratuities, I was dealing strictly with the business of the department.

I am vitally interested
in the question of colonization, because my riding has shown the greatest improvement in this respect of any district in Canada. During the last ten years the number of occupied farms in Cochrane county has increased from 274 to 2,490. Last year I endeavoured to obtain the information now being asked for by hon. members, but I was unable to do so. Will the minister advise the committee how many pe'ople have been settled in North Timiskaming?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I am sorry I am unable
to give the information asked for by the hon. member, and unless a resurvey were made to divide Canada into ridings for the purpose, I doubt if it could be supplied. The following figures show the number placed between October 1, 1930, and February 29, 1932:
British Columbia	 70
Alberta	 1,360
Saskatchewan	 696
Manitoba	 904
Ontario	 2,567
Quebec		127
Maritime provinces	 431
I have examined the reports of the railways and I find them to be very accurate. The families placed by the Canadian National Railways number 2,894; by the Canadian Pacific Railway, 2,471, and by the department, 987. The single men placed by the Canadian National Railways number 2,983; by the Canadian Pacific Railway, 4,331 and by the department, 6,155. These figures cover the same period to which I have referred, from October 1, 1930 to February 29, 1932. On the basis of five members to a family, 45,229 individuals have been absorbed in agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, I still maintain I am not receiving the information for which I have been looking for the last two years and to which I am entitled. The hon. minister has just stated that those who have been placed on farms would not like to have their names shouted from the housetops, but this government has been going up and down the country boasting of its wonderful back to the land policy. The hon. minister has just stated that 50,000 people have been placed on farms without any assistance from the government, but I maintain that to do that is humanly impossible. The minister knows that in northern Ontario the settlers will require provincial or federal aid before they will be

Supply-Immigration
able to seed their land. People cannot be taken from the cities and placed on the land without assistance from the government, especially with the present low prices being received for farm products. If the government sees fit to announce this policy throughout the length and breadth of this country, it should furnish the information to which the committee is entitled. There is no back to the land scheme which is workable under present conditions without aid from either the provincial or the dominion government. I have received hundreds of letters asking for federal aid, and the government owes it to the committee to announce a clear and definite policy in connection with land settlement. Mention is made of abandoned farms, but there must be some reason why those farms were abandoned- there is no doubt that the original holders could not make a living. It would be impossible to take people from the cities and place them upon the .land in northern Ontario without governmental aid. I shall not criticize, but will support any movement which will alleviate unemployment in the cities, but I do not want to see the unemployment in the rural districts become worse. I have enough faith in the minister to feel assured that he will do his best to see that this situation is remedied.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I think I have a fair idea of the difficulties being faced by settlers in the riding of the hon. member (Mr. Bradette) as well as throughout Canada generally because incidentally I have come into contact with them for many years. But I should not like his observations to go without some passing comment. I trust the hon. member does not complain because the government has met with a degree of success in having people return to the land on their own money, the government making the way as easy as it could for them, only with advice, I will admit, as to placing them upon the land best suited to them. I trust he will not complain as to the success the department may have attained in that regard.
With respect to settlers in the northern part of Ontario, I know their plight; I am acquainted with their difficulties and I appreciate the courage which they have exhibited throughout this period of depression. I have reason to remember their courage during the past two or three years; I am not unmindful of their wants; I am acquainted with the efforts that have been made by both the Quebec and the Ontario government to assist them while they have been cleaning up their farms. I do not. need to tell the hon. member that those settlers will receive most sympathetic support.

May I ask the minister
whether the list he just read showing the returns to the farm by provinces, includes all he has in mind? If it does, I may say that he has given no figures showing 50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The figures-and this is all I have said in the house or out of it- including the units of families together with single men, would amount, as of April 2, to 44,959. That is being increased each week. This is on the basis of five to each family.
That does not agree with the figures the minister read for his province.
He gave figures of families.

I noticed the minister quoted the figures for the various provinces. The other night, when the hon. member for Saskatoon was speaking, I think on the Unemployment and Farm Relief bill, he read from some letters that he had received from settlers that had been placed in Meadow Lake, north of Battleford, showing how successful they had been. I know the country into which those people went and I know a number of people who have gone in there and done well; but all the people I know that have gone into the northern portions of Saskatchewan have been those driven out of the south because of the conditions existing there. If the minister is counting those people-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member I am not.

I have watched the
migrations of those people in the last two years. Situated as I am on the west centre of Saskatchewan, I have seen hundreds of them go in. Is it the intention of the government, now that they are placing them on abandoned farms, as the minister has stated-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Not only on abandoned farms-on any farms available, or crown lands.

The only farms available to-day in Saskatchewan are either homesteads along the northern fringe of settlement or abandoned farms, because you cannot sell a farm; if the minister knows where he can make any sales, I wish he would let me know.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I am making them every day. If the hon. member has a farm to sell, let him place it with me.

We are dealing with immigration of British boys. I listened to the hon. member for Dauphin give as his reason why we should go, as we say in Scotch, "very canny" at this time, the approach of thp
Canada Power Corporation

imperial conference. I am of the same opinion that we should go "very canny," but not for that reason. Looking at the question from the boys' viewpoint, I do not think this is any time to bring a boy from Great Britain into conditions such as prevail in Canada to-day. I might tell the minister it is just twenty-six years ago to-day since I left the Clyde, but the day I reached Canada conditions were very different from what they are now and any boy coming from Great Britain at this time will find the struggle much harder than did those of us who came here when I did.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The hon. member is too modest.

I ana not. There are hundreds who have done the same as I. I urge the government to go very slowly in inviting those boys to come to Canada at this time. Like the hon. member for Bow River and for the same reason, I know many of them and get close to them because I am a fellow countryman. We have travelled the road they will have to travel if they come here.

The minister said that he had not given any assistance in a financial way. Has he received any request from the provinces to help to place on the land some of the experienced farmers who are unemployed? I quite agree that land in some places is available. If such a request were to come to him, would his department be willing to consider it in view of the fact that in any case they have to keep most of these people?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The question of giving state aid to colonization-and it has been a subject that many countries in the western hemisphere have undertaken-is one that requires a great deal of consideration. We in Canada have from time to time given aid; shortly after the war we started on rather an elaborate program of state-aided settlement. In view of the present situation the success of that is very difficult to measure. When the program of the department became known with respect to reestablishing people on the farms where they would at least be able to look after themselves in a modest kind of way, many requests came in from all kinds of societies and even at times from provinces, outlining schemes whereby people could be put on the land and be state-aided with money. This is a matter that would require most careful consideration. When I started out to try to reestablish people on the land, my viewpoint was that we would take 
people from the cities, get them off the unemployment shelves and make them selfsupporting.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
